units.title: Skin across a lifetime, hormonal context, and the environments it lives in

lessons.title: What actually changes with age, and which claims change differently
lessons.explanation: Ageing is not one process, and the difference matters commercially as much as biologically. Chronological, or intrinsic, ageing is the slow programme of cell and matrix change that happens to everyone; photoageing is the additional, cumulative damage from ultraviolet exposure and other external insults, and the two proceed together so that what a learner sees in the mirror is always a sum rather than either part alone. The ageing review used in this lesson states the distinction plainly: loss of function and structural stability proceeds unavoidably with age, the result of intrinsic and extrinsic processes that contribute simultaneously to a progressive loss of skin integrity, and extrinsic insults from the environment add to the dermatological signs of ageing. The public-health description is more concrete and more useful for planning: with age the outer layer of the skin gets thinner, paler and less stretchy, blood vessels become more fragile so older adults bruise more easily, and older adults may produce less sweat and oil from the glands in their skin. Two further inputs are named on that page and are routinely left out of cosmetic marketing: hormonal changes such as those at menopause can make skin thinner and drier, and chronic conditions more common in later life, including diabetes, kidney disease and heart disease, can have skin effects of their own. The mechanism review supplies one of the few hard numbers in this area, noting that global lipid content of aged skin is reduced by as much as 65 percent, alongside a reduction in the natural water and fat emulsion on the skin and in stratum corneum water content. That single figure explains most of the subjective experience of mature skin, because a thinner lipid phase means a leakier barrier, which means both more water loss and more reactivity to whatever is applied. From this, three planning consequences follow. First, the measurable changes are mostly about thinning, dryness, fragility and slower recovery, so the interventions with the largest expected effect are boring ones: gentler cleansing, generous moisturising, protection from ultraviolet radiation, and shorter, cooler washing. Second, some changes are outside the reach of any cosmetic step, because a topical product cannot rebuild a dermal collagen framework or restore a lost capillary network; a routine can improve water content, barrier function, tolerance and photoprotection, and that is a real but bounded list. Third, the words used to sell against these changes are not standardised. 'Anti-ageing' is a marketing category rather than a regulatory one, and the course flags it as a term with no shared definition, exactly like 'cosmeceutical'. This lesson teaches what the evidence describes and how to plan around it; it is education, not a treatment plan, and a new, changing, bleeding or non-healing lesion, or a sore that will not close, is a clinical question rather than a cosmetic one.
lessons.example: Worked example. A learner aged 58 brings a shopping list to a routine audit: a 'collagen-boosting' serum, a retinol night oil, a firming day cream with a peptide blend, and a body lotion, and asks which will reverse thinning. Do not answer the purchase question first; convert the list into a map of measured change against influence. Draw three columns. Column one, measured change: epidermis thinner and paler; fewer sweat and oil glands active; global lipid content down by as much as 65 percent in aged skin; more fragile vessels; loss of elastin and collagen; drier skin that loses water more easily. Column two, what a facial routine can influence: hydration and water retention, barrier function and therefore reactivity, tolerance, and protection from further ultraviolet damage. Column three, what no topical step reaches: dermal collagen architecture, capillary networks, and sebaceous or sweat gland number. Now put the four products into column two or three. The retinoid and the peptides are aimed at column three, which is the honest reason to hold a routine's promises low for them: a cosmetic vehicle can change surface water and barrier behaviour quickly, and can at best influence appearance over months, but it cannot rebuild a dermal framework. The body lotion is the one product that addresses a measured change directly, so it moves to the front of the plan. Then do the arithmetic that makes the boring steps visible. Suppose the learner's usual bath is 20 minutes and a shorter one is 10 minutes: at daily bathing that is 7,300 minutes a year against 3,650, a difference of 3,650 minutes, or about 61 hours, or roughly two and a half days of the year that the skin spends wet, warm and surfactant-exposed. That is a larger and better-supported lever than any of the four products, and it is free. The corrected plan: a gentle, fragrance-free cleanser, a moisturiser applied to damp skin at a generous dose, daily broad-spectrum sunscreen, the shorter bath, and skin examination habits because the risk of skin cancer and pre-cancerous growths rises from around age 50. Then, and only then, one product from the list may be trialled as a substitution, with an observable endpoint and a stop rule from lesson 42.
lessons.question: A learner in their late 50s wants to know which serum will reverse age-related thinning of the skin. Which reading matches the mechanism?
lessons.answer: Thinning, dryness and fragility are the measured changes, and a routine can only influence hydration, barrier function, tolerance and protection, so the reliable levers are gentler washing, moisturising and photoprotection
lessons.distractor: A collagen serum can rebuild the dermal framework if it is used for long enough, so the priority is choosing the highest-strength product and applying it twice daily
lessons.correction: The ageing reviews describe thinner skin, reduced lipid content, fewer active oil and sweat glands, and loss of dermal collagen and elastin, with intrinsic and extrinsic processes acting together. A cosmetic step can change surface water content and barrier behaviour, which is real and quick, but it cannot rebuild dermal architecture or restore gland numbers. That is why the defensible plan is gentler washing, a generous moisturiser on damp skin, and photoprotection, with any product added afterwards as one substitution with a written stop rule.

depth.definitions: Intrinsic, or chronological, ageing is the time-dependent programme of change in skin structure and function; extrinsic ageing is damage accumulated from the environment, dominated by ultraviolet radiation from the sun and by smoking. Photoageing is the extrinsic component attributable to light. The stratum corneum is the outer, dead, lipid-rich layer that limits water loss; its water content is what most moisturisers change first. Sebum is the oily secretion of sebaceous glands; xerosis is the clinical word for dry skin. Elastosis describes the abnormal, thickened elastic tissue characteristic of sun-damaged skin. Menopause is the cessation of menstruation and the associated decline in circulating oestrogen. 'Anti-ageing' and 'cosmeceutical' are marketing terms with no separate legal meaning in the United States, and this course flags both. Barrier function means the skin's ability to keep water in and irritants out. A non-healing lesion means a sore or spot that has not healed within the expected time and is a referral trigger rather than a skincare problem.
depth.mechanism: Two mechanisms produce the visible picture, and they are worth keeping separate because they respond to different inputs. The intrinsic route is a slow change in programmes and populations: keratinocyte turnover slows, the epidermis becomes thinner, the lipid mixture between corneocytes changes in both amount and composition, and the dermal collagen and elastin framework loses organisation and quantity. The review cited here reports global lipid content in aged skin reduced by as much as 65 percent, a reduction in the natural water and fat emulsion, and lower stratum corneum water content, which together raise transepidermal water loss and make the surface less able to buffer applied substances. Glandular output falls too, so there is less surface oil and less sweat, which is why mature skin can be simultaneously dry and easily irritated. Vascular walls become more fragile, which is why bruising appears with minor trauma. The extrinsic route is cumulative injury: ultraviolet exposure generates reactive oxygen species and DNA damage that accelerate the same endpoints, so a person's apparent skin age depends heavily on lifetime exposure. Two limits belong here. First, the numbers available are mostly population averages from small studies, not individual predictions, so a given learner may sit far from the average. Second, the skin also reflects systemic health and medication: the public-health page used here names diabetes, kidney disease, heart disease and certain medicines as conditions whose symptoms can show on the skin, and diuretics and other drugs are commonly associated with dryness. That is why a sudden change in skin behaviour deserves a clinician rather than a stronger moisturiser, and why this course never converts a population finding into a personal prognosis.
depth.secondExample: Contrasting cases in which the same vocabulary describes different problems. Case one: a 34-year-old who runs outdoors at midday without sunscreen and now has mottled pigmentation, coarse texture and a few fine lines. Here the extrinsic component dominates, the endpoint to protect is future damage rather than existing texture, and the plan is photoprotection plus a gentle routine; the marketing list aimed at 'ageing' is largely irrelevant because the driver is ongoing exposure. Case two: a 78-year-old taking a diuretic who describes itching, dry scaly legs and easy bruising, and whose skin feels tight after bathing. The changes are real, but the framing shifts: medication and skin disease have to be considered, the itch is a symptom to be assessed rather than a dryness to be scrubbed, and the plan is a clinician conversation plus the same boring basics done properly. Case three: a 61-year-old whose 'dryness' is confined to the lower legs in winter, with a fine cracked pattern like a dried riverbed. That pattern is asteatotic eczema, an inflammatory condition rather than ordinary dryness, and it does not resolve with a lighter lotion. The same three-column map produces three different first actions, and in two of the three the highest-yield step is not a product at all.
depth.mistake: The dominant error is treating slower turnover as a reason to exfoliate more: if cells turn over more slowly, the reasoning goes, they must be removed by force, so mature skin gets acids, scrubs and cleansing brushes at frequencies chosen for younger or oilier skin. The consequence is predictable, because a thinner epidermis with less surface lipid has less reserve, and the stinging that follows is then read as proof that the products are working. The second error is equating wrinkles with dryness, which leads to layered moisturisers where one adequate dose would do, and to disappointment when plumpness that lasts an hour is taken as the expected change. The third is the category error: buying by aisle label, so a product marketed for 'mature skin' is assumed to contain something specific for ageing, when the category itself is a marketing construction. Diagnose your own reasoning with three questions. Which measured change does this step address, and is that change inside or outside the reach of a topical product? What would I observe, over what window, that would tell me it worked? And is anything here a clinical signal, such as a new or changing lesion, a sore that will not heal, unexplained bruising, or itching without a rash? Any yes to the third question moves the work from routine design to a clinician, because the skin is an organ that reports on the rest of the body.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Build a three-column ageing map for one real person, drawing only on what you can observe and record. Column one, measured change: name each change in physical terms (thin, dry, less elastic, bruising easily) rather than in marketing terms (tired, dull, ageing). Column two, routine levers: hydration, barrier function, tolerance, photoprotection, plus the non-product levers of shorter and cooler washing, soft cloths instead of brushes, fragrance-free products, and humidification. Column three, clinical questions: anything new, changing, bleeding, non-healing, painful, blistering, or accompanied by unexplained bruising, itching without a rash, or a systemic illness. Model response: 'Change one: dry, itchy legs in winter, worse after long hot baths. Lever: 10-minute warm bath, gentle fragrance-free cleanser, moisturiser on damp skin twice daily. Change two: faint mottled pigment on the forearms. Lever: daily broad-spectrum sunscreen on the arms as well as the face; no exfoliation. Change three: a scaly patch on the cheek that has been present for three months and sometimes bleeds. Clinical: book an appointment rather than applying anything to it; that is a change with a duration and a symptom.' Self-review rubric, five points: every entry names a physical change rather than a product benefit; every lever is something you can do today without spending more; the plan uses one adequate dose of one moisturiser rather than several layers; the photoprotection step is daily rather than situational; and at least one referral trigger is written down in advance. Note explicitly that no step in the plan claims to restore collagen or thicken skin, because a routine that promises that cannot be evaluated honestly. Reread the same three columns after four weeks and record whether the dry-skin scores moved, which is the only claim the plan should be making.
depth.summary: Ageing skin is a sum of intrinsic change, accumulated extrinsic damage, hormonal shift and general health, and the parts a cosmetic routine can reach are hydration, barrier function, tolerance and protection. Thinning, reduced lipid content, lower glandular output and fragility are the measured changes; 'anti-ageing' is a label rather than a mechanism. Map each observed change to a lever or a clinician, prefer the free levers, and keep promises to the size the evidence supports. The next lesson takes the hormonal component of that map and asks what it changes, what it is claimed to change, and where the line to clinical care sits.

readings.title: National Institute on Aging, Skin Care and Aging (nia.nih.gov) — 'How does skin change as you age?', 'What skin changes should I look out for?', 'How can I protect my skin?'
readings.note: Read the first section for the measured changes: the outer layer getting thinner, paler and less stretchy, more fragile blood vessels and easier bruising, and less sweat and oil from the glands. Note the two inputs cosmetic marketing omits: hormonal change at menopause, and chronic conditions such as diabetes, kidney disease and heart disease that show on the skin. Read 'What skin changes should I look out for?' for the skin-cancer framing and the note that basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma grow slowly and usually appear on sun-exposed sites, and the final section for the protection steps. This is patient-facing government guidance, not a treatment protocol.

readings.title: Farage MA et al., Characteristics of the Aging Skin, Adv Wound Care 2013 (PMC3840548) — Abstract ('Critical Issues') and 'Discussion of Findings and Relevant Literature'
readings.note: Read the Critical Issues abstract for the statement that loss of function and structural stability proceeds unavoidably with age, from intrinsic and extrinsic processes contributing simultaneously, and that falling oestrogen in midlife produces premature ageing relative to similarly aged men. Then read the discussion section for the quantitative anchors used in this lesson: global lipid content of aged skin reduced as much as 65 percent, reduced natural water and fat emulsion, and lower stratum corneum water content. Treat these as reported review findings from a narrative synthesis rather than as individual predictions.

readings.title: American Academy of Dermatology, How to care for your skin in your 60s and 70s (aad.org) — 'Skin becomes drier with age' and the numbered dermatologist recommendations
readings.note: Read the opening of 'Skin becomes drier with age' for the reasons dermatologists give: thinner skin that loses water more easily, plus medications and medical conditions. Then read recommendation 1 in full, which is the source of this lesson's bathing arithmetic (short five- to ten-minute bath or shower, warm rather than hot water, soft cloth instead of a buff puff or bath brush, a gentle fragrance-free moisturising cleanser, and the explicit warning that bath oil increases fall risk), and recommendation 5, which is simply to go fragrance free. The page also notes that skin cancer risk rises from about age 50 and links a self-examination guide.

visual.title: Measured change mapped to levers, with the clinical column separated

Column three holds clinical signals and is drawn behind a barrier line so it is never merged into the routine. Below, a bathing bar chart compares annual minutes spent wet at two bath durations.
steps: Column one, measured change: outer layer thinner, paler, less stretchy; fragile vessels with easier bruising; reduced sweat and oil output; lower stratum corneum water; global lipid content in aged skin reduced by as much as 65 percent.
Inputs arrow into column one from the left: intrinsic programme, cumulative ultraviolet exposure, hormonal change at menopause, and general health or medication.
Column two, routine levers: water content, barrier function, reactivity, tolerance, and photoprotection, each drawn as a small dial a learner can actually turn today.
Non-product lever strip beneath column two: shorter and cooler washing with a soft cloth, one adequate dose of a fragrance-free moisturiser on damp skin, humidification of dry indoor air.

lessons.title: Hormonal context: cycle, pregnancy and perimenopause without the 'hormone-balancing' marketing
lessons.explanation: Hormones genuinely change skin, and the useful skill is telling the documented direction of that change from the products sold as if they controlled it. The evidence base is uneven, and honesty about that unevenness is part of the content. Oestrogen receptors are present throughout the skin, with the highest density in the face, genital region and legs; the receptor subtype seen predominantly in skin is oestrogen receptor beta, and a reduction in circulating oestrogen is associated with a fall in receptor expression. The menopause review used here reports evidence implicating oestrogen in transepidermal water loss and in the reduction of dermal collagen, and describes an increase in collagen content and dermal thickness demonstrated as early as three months after treatment began, reproducible regardless of the route of oestrogen administration. That last finding concerns clinician-directed hormone treatment, not a cosmetic cream, and the review's own management table for postmenopausal itching is a list of general measures rather than products: low-pH emollients at least once daily, nails kept short, use of humidifiers, reduced bathing time, and avoidance of irritants including soap. It also reports that the most commonly observed dermatoses in perimenopausal and menopausal women were eczematous eruptions, including allergic contact dermatitis and asteatotic eczema, with itching frequently seen alongside dry skin. Pregnancy is a different hormonal environment and a different set of tasks. A comprehensive review describes cutaneous change driven by hormonal, mechanical and immunological factors, naming physiological hyperpigmentation, striae gravidarum and vascular alterations, and separating those from pregnancy-specific dermatoses such as pemphigoid gestationis, impetigo herpetiformis and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, which carry risk to mother and fetus and are managed by clinicians. Two planning consequences follow. First, cyclic and life-stage patterns are best handled by observation first and intervention second, because a pattern only becomes a pattern when the observation window spans more than one cycle. Second, 'hormonal' is a marketing word with no shared standard, like 'balancing' or 'detox': a product cannot measure a learner's oestrogen, and no cosmetic ingredient has an established role in normalising circulating hormone levels. This is education about what changes and how to plan around it. It contains no dosing and no treatment advice, and in pregnancy any active ingredient, any prescribed medicine and any new skin problem belongs with the learner's clinician, not with a routine. Referral triggers are explicit below.
lessons.example: Worked example. A learner of 51 asks about a serum advertised to 'rebalance hormones' for dry, itchy skin that began around the time her periods became irregular. Work the problem in four passes. Pass one, mechanism: what is documented is that oestrogen receptors are distributed through skin with the highest density on the face, genital region and legs; that falling circulating oestrogen is associated with reduced receptor expression, increased transepidermal water loss and reduced dermal collagen; and that perimenopausal skin problems are most commonly eczematous eruptions and itching with dryness. None of that is a deficiency a cream can correct from the outside, because a topical product acts on the surface rather than on circulating hormone levels. Pass two, arithmetic on observation windows. A menstrual cycle runs about 28 days, so the 90-day window recommended for judging a cyclic pattern covers 90 divided by 28, which is about 3.2 cycles; two cycles is only 56 days and three cycles 84 days. That is why a two-week trial of anything cannot separate a hormonal pattern from weather, sleep, stress or a new product. Pass three, the competing explanation. Itchy, dry, eczematous skin at this life stage has several documented possibilities, including asteatotic eczema and allergic contact dermatitis, and both are conditions rather than dryness problems. If the learner is also flushing on the cheeks, the rosacea picture belongs in the differential too, and the public-health description of that condition notes that it is more common in middle-aged and older adults and in women, and that it may be underdiagnosed in darker skin because pigment can mask facial redness. Pass four, the plan. Keep the routine to a gentle fragrance-free cleanser, a low-pH emollient applied at least once daily, humidification of the bedroom, shorter warm showers, and daily photoprotection, and log the pattern for three cycles with four fields: date, severity of itching and tightness, cycle day if known, and everything else that changed. Then bring the log to a clinician if the pattern is cyclical and inflammatory, if there are patches that do not respond, or if there is flushing with papules. The product question answers itself: nothing on the list addresses circulating oestrogen, and the documented general measures cost less and have published support.
lessons.question: A learner in perimenopause with dry, itchy, occasionally eczematous skin asks which serum will rebalance her hormones. What is the defensible reading?
lessons.answer: Documented changes are reduced oestrogen-associated collagen and increased water loss with eczematous dryness, so the supported steps are general measures such as a low-pH emollient, humidification and shorter washing, with the pattern logged across about three cycles and a clinician involved if it is inflammatory
lessons.distractor: A topical serum can normalise hormone levels in the skin if it contains phytoestrogens, so a higher concentration is the priority before considering anything else
lessons.correction: Falling oestrogen is associated with reduced receptor expression, higher transepidermal water loss and reduced dermal collagen, and the commonly reported perimenopausal dermatoses are eczematous eruptions and itching with dryness. A surface product does not change circulating hormone levels, and 'hormonal' or 'balancing' are marketing words with no shared standard. A 28-day cycle means a 90-day log covers about 3.2 cycles, which is what makes a cyclic pattern visible, and eczematous skin is a condition with its own causes, including contact allergy, rather than simple dryness.

depth.definitions: Oestrogen receptors are proteins that bind oestrogen and mediate its effects in tissue; two subtypes exist, and the beta subtype predominates in skin. Perimenopause is the transition before menopause, with irregular cycles and fluctuating hormone levels; menopause is defined by the end of menstruation. Hormone replacement therapy is clinician-prescribed treatment, not a cosmetic step. Transepidermal water loss is the outward diffusion of water through the skin and is used as an index of barrier function. Xerosis means dry skin and pruritus means itching. Asteatotic eczema is an inflammatory dry-skin condition with a cracked, paved appearance, often on the lower legs in cold weather. Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed immune reaction to a substance, distinct from irritation. Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is a liver condition of pregnancy associated with severe itching and risk to the fetus. Striae gravidarum are stretch marks arising in pregnancy. 'Hormone-balancing' and 'detoxifying' are marketing phrases with no standardised meaning. Hyperpigmentation of pregnancy is increased pigment, and melasma is a patterned facial pigmentation that can be triggered by hormones and light.
depth.mechanism: Follow the oestrogen pathway to its endpoints. Oestrogen receptors sit in keratinocytes, fibroblasts and blood vessels, so oestrogen signalling influences matrix production, water handling and vascular behaviour simultaneously. When circulating oestrogen falls, receptor expression falls with it, and the reported correlates are increased transepidermal water loss and reduced dermal collagen. That combination is why dryness and laxity so often arrive together in midlife: less collagen means a thinner support structure, while higher water loss and a changed lipid environment mean a drier, more reactive surface. It also explains why the reported repair signal, an increase in collagen content and dermal thickness within about three months of starting oestrogen treatment, comes from systemic treatment rather than from a cream, because the stimulus has to reach fibroblasts through the circulation and across a dermal distance that topical delivery is not designed to cover. Pregnancy runs a different script, because circulating oestrogen, progesterone, placental hormones and mechanical stretch all rise at once: pigmentary change follows from increased melanocyte activity under hormonal stimulation plus light exposure, stretch marks follow from dermal mechanical strain with hormonal contributions to matrix remodelling, and vascular changes follow from increased blood volume and vessel dilation. The limits must be stated with the mechanism. First, the skin-hormone literature is largely observational and heterogeneous, and the review cited here is a narrative synthesis of association rather than a set of controlled causal findings. Second, oestrogen is not the only driver: mechanical stretch in pregnancy and photoexposure in both situations contribute independently, which is why different learners with similar hormone profiles end up with different skin. Third, nothing in this pathway recommends, doses or substitutes for hormone treatment, and any such decision belongs to a clinician who knows the person's history and risk profile, including contraindications.
depth.secondExample: Contrasting lifecycle cases to show that the same word requires different actions. Case one: a 26-year-old who notices one or two inflamed spots in the week before her period and nothing else. The pattern is consistent, low severity and not scarring; the correct response is a cycle log with the four fields from the example, gentle routine care, and no escalation of actives, because nothing here needs a hormonal workup and the pattern already has an explanation. Case two: a 30-year-old, 29 weeks pregnant, who develops symmetrical brown patches on the cheeks and a dark line on the abdomen, and asks about a lightening product she found online. The pigment is a documented physiological change of pregnancy driven by hormonal and other factors, so the plan is photoprotection with a tinted, iron-oxide-containing broad-spectrum sunscreen from lesson 53, gentle products, and patience, and the online product is a hard no: the dermatology public guidance cited in the next lesson reports that researchers have found steroids or mercury that were not on the label in imported skin-care products, and that prolonged unlabelled steroid use can thin and permanently discolour skin. Any new treatment decision in pregnancy goes to her clinician. Case three: a 52-year-old with severe itching in the third trimester of a pregnancy, with no rash. That is not a routine-tuning problem at all: cholestasis of pregnancy presents as itching and carries fetal risk, so the action is urgent clinical contact rather than any product. Same life stage vocabulary, three different actions, and in two of the three the useful intervention is not on a shelf.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur. The first is believing that a topical product can adjust a systemic hormone pattern, which the physiology rules out, and which marketing language such as 'balancing' or 'hormonal support' is designed to imply without evidence. The second is attributing every midlife skin change to hormones, when the differential includes ordinary dryness from heating, contact allergy from a product the learner has used for years, asteatotic eczema, rosacea, thyroid and other medical conditions, and medication side effects; that shortcut causes learners to treat a condition with moisturiser for months. The third is the pregnancy shortcut in both directions: assuming that because a product is sold freely it is appropriate during pregnancy, and assuming that everything must stop, including care a clinician has prescribed, which creates its own problems. Diagnose your own reasoning with three questions. What would I expect to observe, and over how many cycles or weeks, if this were the hormonal pattern I think it is? Which competing explanation has not been excluded, particularly contact allergy from a product that has been in use for a long time? And is there any red flag, such as itching in pregnancy without a rash, a rapidly enlarging or painful lesion, blistering, or a rash that spreads? A yes to the third question is urgent clinical contact, and the whole framing of this lesson is education rather than diagnosis or treatment.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Start a three-cycle skin log with five columns and no product changes for the duration. Column one, date; column two, cycle day or weeks since the last period; column three, the two symptoms you will actually rate (for example itching and tightness) on a simple 0 to 3 scale; column four, the routine as performed, including whether the learner bathed longer than usual; column five, everything else that changed, such as travel, heating, a new laundry detergent or a stressful week. Model response: 'Days 1 to 5, tightness 2, itching 1, routine as usual, nothing else changed. Day 19, tightness 3 and a fine cracked patch on the left shin after a 25-minute hot bath; noted the bath as the only change. Day 27, tightness 1.' Self-review rubric, five points: at least 56 days and ideally 84 days are logged, which covers two to three cycles; the ratings are defined in advance so they mean the same thing each time; every competing change is recorded rather than remembered; no active or treatment is started, stopped or escalated during the window; and the plan's first steps are the general measures, namely a low-pH emollient at least once daily, humidification, shorter warm washing, and avoidance of soap on the affected areas. Then write the referral conditions in advance: itching in pregnancy without a rash, severe itching with no explanation, a rash that spreads or blisters, facial flushing with papules, or patches that do not improve after several weeks of general measures. Take the log with you, because a dated record is more useful than a reconstruction, and if a clinician has prescribed something, it stays exactly as prescribed while the log runs.
depth.summary: Hormones change skin through documented routes, principally oestrogen's influence on collagen and water loss and the pigmentary, mechanical and vascular changes of pregnancy, and those routes respond to general measures and, where clinically appropriate, to clinician-directed treatment rather than to cosmetics. Log before intervening, cover two to three cycles, hold competing explanations open, and treat the words 'hormonal' and 'balancing' as marketing. Pregnancy adds a hard boundary with its own referral triggers. The next lesson moves from hormonal variation to a variable that changes the entire risk calculus: how much melanin the skin makes and how it responds to injury.

readings.title: Menopause, skin and common dermatoses. Part 2: skin disorders, Clin Exp Dermatol 2022 (PMC10092853) — Introduction, 'Changes in skin structure after menopause' (Collagen), 'Xerosis, pruritus and dermatitis' and Table 3
readings.note: Read the Introduction for the receptor anatomy: oestrogen receptors throughout the skin with the highest density in the face, genital region and legs, oestrogen receptor beta predominating in skin, and reduced circulating oestrogen associated with a fall in receptor expression. Read the Collagen subsection for the reported increase in collagen content and dermal thickness within about three months of treatment, reproducible across routes, and note that this concerns clinician-directed hormone treatment rather than cosmetics. Read 'Xerosis, pruritus and dermatitis' for the finding that eczematous eruptions, including allergic contact dermatitis and asteatotic eczema, were the most commonly reported dermatoses in perimenopausal and menopausal women, and read Table 3 as a list of general measures (low-pH emollients at least once daily, short nails, humidifiers, reduced bathing time, avoidance of irritants including soap). This is a narrative review of association, not a treatment protocol, and the article is behind a Wiley route that may present a check to automated tools; the abstract, headings and the quoted sections were retrievable by text extraction when this pack was authored.

readings.title: Cutaneous Changes During Pregnancy: A Comprehensive Review, Cureus 2024 (PMC11497768) — Abstract, the Review body on physiological changes and pregnancy-specific dermatoses, and the note on the drug table
readings.note: Read the Abstract for the framing that cutaneous change in pregnancy is driven by hormonal, mechanical and immunological factors, and for the split between physiological changes such as hyperpigmentation, striae gravidarum and vascular alterations, and pathological conditions such as pemphigoid gestationis, impetigo herpetiformis and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Read the body for the statement that intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is thought to arise from genetic, hormonal and environmental factors, and for the sentence that pregnancy-specific dermatoses such as these can pose risks to both mother and fetus if not managed properly. Note that the article includes a table of preferred drugs in pregnancy; that table is clinician material and is cited here only as evidence that treatment choices in pregnancy are clinician decisions rather than cosmetic ones. No dose, drug or schedule from this article is used in this course.

readings.title: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases, Rosacea (niams.nih.gov) — 'Overview of Rosacea' and 'Who Gets Rosacea?'
readings.note: Read the Overview for the definition of rosacea as a long-term inflammatory skin condition causing reddened skin and a rash, usually on the nose and cheeks, with symptoms that come and go and factors such as sun and emotional stress bringing them on, and for the statement that there is no cure but treatment can keep it under control. Read 'Who Gets Rosacea?' for the group profile used in this lesson's differential: middle-aged and older adults, women more often though men tend to be more severely affected, and fair skin more often with the explicit note that it may be underdiagnosed in darker-skinned people because darker skin can mask facial redness. visual.title: One word, three life stages, three plans
visual.description: A three-lane lifecycle diagram. Each lane carries the circulatory hormone signal at the top, the documented skin endpoints in the middle, and the action list at the bottom. A cycle-wheel inset shows a 28-day cycle with a 90-day observation bracket drawn across it, and a hard boundary line marks where clinical contact replaces routine design.
steps: Lane 1, cyclical: hormone signal drawn as a monthly wave; endpoints limited to documented pigmentation and sebum-influenced variation; action list is a log with date, cycle day, rated symptoms, routine as performed, and other changes.

Cycle-wheel inset: 28-day cycle marked, with brackets at 56 days (two cycles) and 84 days (three cycles) and a 90-day label reading about 3.2 cycles, showing why short trials cannot read a cyclic pattern.

Lane 2, pregnancy: rising hormonal, mechanical and immunological arrows; endpoints labelled hyperpigmentation, striae gravidarum and vascular change; a separate red-bordered box lists pregnancy-specific dermatoses as clinician territory, with itching without a rash flagged as an urgent contact.

Lane 3, perimenopause and menopause: falling oestrogen with reduced receptor expression; endpoints labelled increased transepidermal water loss, reduced dermal collagen, and eczematous dryness with itching; action list is the general-measures row from the review's management table.

Marketing term strip across all three lanes: 'hormonal', 'balancing', 'phytoestrogen support', each struck through and labelled no shared standard, with a note that no topical step changes circulating hormone levels.

Boundary line at the right edge: a clinician gate listing pregnancy-active decisions, itching without rash, severe unexplained itching, spreading or blistering rash, flushing with papules, and any new or changing lesion.

lessons.title: Skin of colour: why pigment, scarring and the sunscreen question run differently
lessons.explanation: Melanin does two things at once, and the second one is the reason this lesson exists. It absorbs ultraviolet and visible radiation, which is protective, and the same machinery is capable of an exaggerated response to trouble, which is why the common pigmentary and scarring problems of darker skin are different in frequency and in behaviour rather than merely in degree. The reference review used here states the position directly: post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is a common consequence of inflammatory skin disease that tends to affect darker-skinned patients with greater frequency and severity, and epidemiological studies show that disorders of pigmentation, including post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, are among the most common reasons darker racial and ethnic groups consult a dermatologist. The mechanism is described in two layers. When the pigment sits in the epidermis, there is an increase in the production and transfer of melanin into surrounding keratinocytes, and although the exact mechanism is unknown, this rise in melanocyte activity has been shown to be stimulated by prostanoids, cytokines and chemokines, by reactive oxygen species released during inflammation, and by specific mediators including leukotrienes such as LTC4 and LTD4, prostaglandins E2 and D2, thromboxane-2, interleukin-1, interleukin-6, tumour necrosis factor alpha, and epidermal growth factor. When the pigment sits in the dermis, inflammation has damaged basal keratinocytes, which release large amounts of melanin that is then taken up by macrophages, now called melanophages, in the upper dermis, producing a blue-grey colour at the site; and the review notes that topical therapy is typically effective for epidermal pigment while dermal pigment behaves differently. Two practical consequences follow immediately. First, the driver to remove is the inflammation, so the order of operations is to treat the cause and protect from light rather than to attack the mark. Second, the treatment timeline is measured in months and is often partial, because pigment is cleared by cell turnover and by the slow removal of dermal pigment. Scarring runs on a parallel track. In darker-pigmented populations, keloid incidence is reported in the range of 4.5 to 16 percent, with higher incidence during pregnancy and puberty and increased risk with a family history, and keloids are triggered by ordinary events including acne, piercings, surgery, insect bites, burns, lacerations and vaccination. A keloid is distinguished from a hypertrophic scar by extending beyond the site of the original injury. It is benign, and treatment is directed at symptoms or cosmetic concerns, which places it firmly in clinical hands. Sunscreen is the third strand, and here the misunderstanding is often reversed: skin of colour is at risk of skin cancer and photoageing, and pigmentary disorders worsened by ultraviolet exposure are a leading reason for dermatology visits, yet a cited consumer barrier to consistent use is the white residue left by many products, which is a formulation and adherence problem rather than a need problem. Public guidance recommends a tinted sunscreen containing iron oxide, because iron oxide protects against visible light, which is a documented driver of dark spots, together with SPF 30 or higher, broad-spectrum protection, water resistance, and a shade that blends with the skin tone. This lesson is education. It teaches why the questions differ, how to plan, and which signals end cosmetic care and become clinical care.
lessons.example: Worked example. A learner with medium-brown skin has flat brown marks at the sites of old spots, one raised firm nodule on the shoulder from a piercing, and a history of acne that still flares twice a month. They ask which lightening serum removes the marks and whether they can scrub them away. Work it in four steps. Step one, classify by tissue. The flat brown marks are post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, most likely epidermal because they are flat and brown rather than blue-grey, so topical care can plausibly help over months; the raised nodule is a scar, possibly keloidal, which no serum addresses and which needs assessment; the active acne is the engine still running, and until it stops, new marks will keep forming, because each inflamed lesion releases the mediators that increase melanocyte activity. Step two, quantify what the learner is up against. Reported keloid incidence in darker-pigmented populations is 4.5 to 16 percent, so if we take the top and the bottom of that range, the upper figure is 16 divided by 4.5, roughly 3.6 times the lower one: the literature is describing a wide spread rather than a single number, and no individual can read their own risk off it. For the pigment side, the systematic review of prevention in skin of colour screened 3,205 articles, reviewed 261 in full text and included 14 studies covering 369 participants, which works out at about 26 participants per study on average; that is enough to generate hypotheses and far too little to support a confident personal claim about which single intervention prevents marks. Step three, set honest expectations from the source: hyperpigmentation is described as treatable but not curable, because new marks can form even after existing ones fade, which makes prevention the durable half of the plan. Step four, write the plan. Treat the acne, which is a clinician conversation if it is scarring or persistent; use a tinted broad-spectrum sunscreen with iron oxide at SPF 30 or higher, reapplied every two hours outdoors and after sweating or swimming; keep the routine gentle, since irritation itself creates more pigment, and the guidance is explicit that a product which burns or stings should be stopped; avoid imported lightening creams of unknown provenance, because the public guidance cites researchers finding steroids and mercury that were not on the label in imported skin-care products, with prolonged unlabelled steroid use capable of thinning skin and causing permanent discolouration; and bring the shoulder nodule to a clinician rather than trying to flatten it. No scrubbing, no bleaching, no stacking of three pigment products.
lessons.question: A learner with darker skin and flat brown marks from old spots asks how to remove them, and mentions they plan to scrub and to buy an imported lightening cream. Which set of corrections reflects the mechanism and the verified guidance?
lessons.answer: Treat and prevent the inflammation that drives pigment, protect with a tinted iron-oxide broad-spectrum sunscreen, keep the routine gentle, expect months with possible new marks, avoid unlabelled imported lightening products, and have any raised scar assessed clinically
lessons.distractor: Scrubbing removes the pigmented surface cells and the imported cream speeds the process, so the correct plan is daily exfoliation until the marks lighten and a stronger imported product for the residue
lessons.correction: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation follows inflammation through mediators that raise melanocyte activity, so irritation adds pigment rather than removing it; scrubbing is a new inflammatory stimulus. The public guidance recommends beginning with sunscreen, specifically a tinted product with iron oxide for visible light, plus SPF 30 or higher and broad-spectrum coverage, and states that dark spots are treatable but not curable because new ones can form. Imported products have been found to contain steroids and mercury not declared on the label, with thinning and permanent discolouration as consequences. Raised firm scars are a different tissue and belong to a clinician.

depth.definitions: Melanin is the pigment produced by melanocytes; melanosomes are the organelles that carry it and are transferred into keratinocytes. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is excess pigment at the site of prior inflammation or injury. Epidermal pigment is brown and relatively diffuse; dermal pigment, produced when inflammation damages basal keratinocytes, is taken up by macrophages known as melanophages and appears blue-grey and deeper. Fitzpatrick skin phototypes classify pigmentary response and are the reason skin of colour is often described as types IV to VI. A keloid is a raised scar extending beyond the original injury; a hypertrophic scar stays within it. Iron oxide is a pigment used in tinted sunscreens that blocks visible light in addition to ultraviolet. Visible light is the part of the spectrum that reaches the dermis and is a documented aggravator of pigmentary disorders. A test spot is a small supervised trial on a limited area before treating a larger area, used when a procedure carries pigmentary risk. 'Brightening', 'evening' and 'lightening' are marketing words without a shared standard, and in the United States a product that lightens pigment by interfering with melanin synthesis is generally being marketed with a drug-type claim rather than only a cosmetic one.
depth.mechanism: Why darker skin responds this way is a question about amplification rather than sensitivity. Melanocytes in more pigmented skin are not simply more numerous; the pigmentary apparatus is more active and the transfer machinery carries more melanin into keratinocytes, so the same inflammatory signal produces a larger output. The mediators listed in the review are the same ones any inflamed lesion releases, which is why an insect bite, a burn, a pimple or a hair-removal injury can each leave a mark, and why the cause of the inflammation matters more than the mark's appearance. Epidermal pigment clears as keratinocytes are replaced, which is a matter of months and is why topical therapy is described as typically effective for that layer. Dermal pigment follows a different path: basal keratinocyte damage releases pigment into the dermis, where it is engulfed by melanophages that turn over far more slowly, producing the blue-grey tint and the poor response to topical agents. Keloid formation is a third mechanism again, and the keloid reference describes it as aberrant wound healing in which the fibroblastic phase of healing continues unchecked, driven by overactive fibroblasts producing large amounts of collagen and growth factors, with classic histological findings of large hyalinised collagen bundles. Two limits must be stated with the mechanism. First, the mediator list comes from a review of studies in cells, tissue and patients rather than from a single causal experiment, so it explains plausibility rather than predicting individual outcomes. Second, intervention does not erase the mechanism: because the amplifying apparatus remains, prevention of new inflammation is not a secondary goal but the main one, and that is exactly what the public guidance means when it says hyperpigmentation is not curable but can be prevented from developing again. Nothing here is a procedure recommendation, and any decision to use a prescription-strength agent, a peel or a laser in pigmented skin belongs to a clinician who can weigh the risk of treatment-induced pigmentation.
depth.secondExample: Contrasting cases in which the same ingredient list has a different meaning. Case one: a fair-skinned learner with sun-induced freckling and mottled pigment on the forearms who never burns badly and does not wear sunscreen. Here the driver is chronic ultraviolet exposure on photodamaged skin, the endpoint is preventing further damage and screening for lesions, and a tinted sunscreen with iron oxide is useful but the priority is habitual daily protection on the sites that actually get exposed. Case two: a learner with deep brown skin who has just finished treating severe acne and now has extensive marks. The driver was the inflammation, which has stopped, so the marks will fade slowly on their own; the same sunscreen matters more for the visible-light component, because protecting from visible light is what is described as helping to prevent and clear dark spots, and the risk calculus for any procedural option is different again because of pigmentary risk. Case three: a learner with a strong family history of keloids who asks whether a cosmetic procedure is a good idea for a small scar. Reported incidence in darker-pigmented populations sits at 4.5 to 16 percent with higher risk in pregnancy and puberty, and family history increases risk, so the answer is not a product recommendation but a question for a clinician who understands scar-prone skin and can discuss options and their risks. Case four: a person who uses a skin-lightening product of unknown origin and develops thinning and new darkening. That pattern, in the public guidance, is a described consequence of unlabelled steroids; the action is to stop and seek clinical assessment, not to switch brands.
depth.mistake: Four errors dominate. The first is the protection paradox: because melanin is protective, learners and sometimes sellers conclude that darker skin does not need sunscreen, when the cited study's introduction states that patients with skin of colour are at risk for skin cancer and photoageing and are uniquely predisposed to pigmentary disorders worsened by ultraviolet exposure. The second is treating pigment with irritation, which includes scrubbing, strong acids and stacked actives; each irritant event is a fresh inflammatory stimulus feeding the pathway that produced the mark. The third is buying on the strength of the words, where 'brightening', 'whitening', 'lightening' and 'glow' carry no shared definition, and where the products most likely to produce fast visible change are those that contain undeclared actives; the guidance names steroids and mercury in imported products as a real hazard with permanent consequences. The fourth is collapsing three different tissues into one complaint, so that a raised keloidal scar, flat epidermal pigment and blue-grey dermal pigment are all expected to respond to one serum. Diagnose your own reasoning with four questions. Is the inflammation still active, and if so, what treats it? Is the mark flat or raised, brown or blue-grey, because that predicts response? What is protecting the site from ultraviolet and visible light, and is the product tinted with iron oxide? And has any product been used that is not fully labelled in a language and jurisdiction I can verify? Any raised, painful or rapidly enlarging scar, any new or changing skin lesion, and any pigmentation accompanied by systemic symptoms or by a new medicine should go to a clinician, and in the United States a suspected problem with a cosmetic can also be reported to the regulator as described in lesson 42.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Build a pigment audit for one real site over four weeks and change nothing else in the window. Columns: lesion site; trigger you can identify (acne, insect bite, hair removal, burn, friction, medication); appearance (flat brown, blue-grey, raised, mixed); duration; whether the driver is still active; and what is being done for ultraviolet and visible-light protection. Then add one column for the referral flags. Model response: 'Left cheek, three flat brown marks, all at old acne sites, driver active because acne still flares weekly, four months old, daily tinted iron-oxide sunscreen SPF 50 with reapplication midday. Action: clinician appointment about the persistent acne rather than a new pigment product, because the marks will recur while the driver runs. Right shoulder, one raised firm nodule at a piercing site, six months old, larger than the original piercing, sometimes itchy. Referral flag: raised scar extending beyond the injury site. Action: clinical assessment, no attempt to flatten it at home.' Self-review rubric, five points: every entry names a physical driver and a tissue type rather than a product benefit; no irritant step is present in the plan, including scrubs, strong acids and brushes; the photoprotection entry names a tinted product with iron oxide, SPF 30 or higher, broad-spectrum, plus a reapplication rule; the plan states honestly that fading takes months and that new marks can form; and at least one referral trigger is written down, covering raised or painful scars, a new or changing lesion, rapidly darkening pigment, or pigmentation that appeared with a new medicine. Then re-check the same sites at four weeks and record only what changed, which is a measurement rather than a hope, and remember this exercise is education and not a substitute for assessment of anything raised, changing, bleeding or painful.
depth.summary: In skin of colour the pigmentary apparatus amplifies the response to injury, so the causal chain runs from inflammation to mediators to melanocyte activity to marks that clear slowly, and the only durable plan is to stop the inflammation, protect from ultraviolet and visible light including with iron oxide, avoid irritation, and expect months. Scarring risk also differs, with keloid incidence in darker-pigmented populations reported between 4.5 and 16 percent and ordinary triggers such as acne and piercings implicated. Products sold with the words brightening or lightening have no shared standard, and some imported products have been found to contain undeclared steroids and mercury. Raised, changing or painful lesions leave this course and enter clinical care. The next lesson follows the same logic out of the bathroom and into work, where hands and sunlight deliver the dose.

readings.title: Davis EC, Callender VD, Postinflammatory Hyperpigmentation: A Review of the Epidemiology, Clinical Features, and Treatment Options in Skin of Color (PMC2921758) — Abstract, Epidemiology, Pathogenesis
readings.note: Read the Abstract for the statements used in this lesson: post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is a common consequence of inflammatory dermatoses that affects darker-skinned patients with greater frequency and severity, dyschromias are among the most common reasons darker racial and ethnic groups consult a dermatologist, treatment should begin early and starts with managing the initial inflammatory condition, first-line therapy typically includes topical depigmenting agents plus photoprotection, topical therapy is typically effective for epidermal pigment, and it can have a significant psychosocial impact with Fitzpatrick types IV to VI affected more often and more severely. Read the Pathogenesis section for the mediator list and for the dermal mechanism: inflammation damages basal keratinocytes, which release melanin that is taken up by macrophages called melanophages in the upper dermis and produces a blue-grey appearance. Note that the treatment sections describe clinician-directed agents; the pack uses only the mechanism and epidemiology, never the regimens.

readings.title: StatPearls, Keloid (NCBI Bookshelf, NBK507899) — Introduction and Epidemiology
readings.note: Read the Introduction for the definitional contrast that matters here, namely that keloidal tissue extends beyond the initial site of trauma whereas normal and hypertrophic scars do not, and for the trigger list (surgery, piercings, acne, tattooing, insect bites, burns, lacerations, abrasions, vaccinations and any other process causing cutaneous inflammation) plus the note that higher incidences are seen in darker-skinned individuals of African, Asian and Hispanic descent. Read the Epidemiology section for the figures quoted: incidence in darker-pigmented populations ranging from 4.5 to 16 percent, notably higher during pregnancy and puberty, and increased risk with a positive family history. Read the Prognosis line stating that keloidal scars are benign and treatment is directed at symptom relief or cosmetic concerns, which is why this course routes them to a clinician rather than a routine. Bookshelf may present a check to automated tools; the abstract, headings and quoted sections were retrievable by text extraction when this pack was authored.

readings.title: Sunscreen recommendations for patients with skin of color in the popular press and in the dermatology clinic (PMC8072489) — Introduction
readings.note: Read the Introduction for the evidence behind this lesson's adherence argument: patients with skin of colour are at risk for skin cancer and photoageing and are uniquely predisposed to pigmentary disorders worsened by ultraviolet exposure; photo-exacerbated pigmentary disorders are among the most common conditions leading to dermatology consultation in patients with darker skin tones; cosmetic elegance is the most important product feature for consumers; and patients with darker skin tones cite undesirable white residue as an impediment to regular use. The paper also reports surveys of popular-press recommendations and of dermatologists, which is useful for seeing how mainstream advice has differed from clinic advice; treat its product-level findings as a snapshot of its own sample rather than as a current recommendation.

readings.title: American Academy of Dermatology, How to fade dark spots in darker skin tones (aad.org) — 'What causes hyperpigmentation?', 'What treatments do dermatologists recommend for hyperpigmentation?', 'Some products that fade dark spots do more harm than good' and 'Is hyperpigmentation curable?'
readings.note: Read 'What causes hyperpigmentation?' for the trigger list (spots appearing when a pimple or patch of psoriasis clears, when a wound from an insect bite, cut or burn heals, with certain medications, when a skin or hair-care product irritates the skin, and with hormonal changes such as pregnancy) and for the treatment logic that the cause must be treated first, with gentle 'for sensitive skin' products recommended and an explicit instruction to stop any product that burns or stings. Read the treatment section for the iron oxide recommendation and the full checklist (SPF 30 or higher, broad-spectrum, water-resistant, non-comedogenic if oily, blends with skin tone to avoid a white cast), including the explanation that iron oxide protects from visible light, described there as a cause of dark spots. Read 'Some products that fade dark spots do more harm than good' for the finding that researchers have identified steroids or mercury that were not listed on the label of imported skin-care products, with thinning, fragility and permanent discolouration as consequences, and 'Is hyperpigmentation curable?' for the honest statement that marks can be removed but new ones can form, making prevention the durable half of the plan.

readings.title: Prevention of Post-Inflammatory Hyperpigmentation in Skin of Colour: A Systematic Review (PMC12062726) — 'Methods 2.2 Search Strategy' and 'Results 3.1 Patient Characteristics'
readings.note: Read the search-strategy paragraph for the screening arithmetic quoted in this lesson's example: title and abstract screening of 3,205 articles, full-text review of 261 articles, and 14 studies ultimately included, summarising 369 patients, with most studies from Thailand (57 percent), Korea (14 percent), the United States, China and Italy (7 percent each). The point of the reading is scale, not conclusion: 14 studies and 369 patients is a small base from which to generalise about prevention in any individual, and this pack therefore cites the review only for the size of the evidence and never for a prevention regimen.
