visual.title: Two patterns that sound alike, and the label trap between them
visual.description: A decision diagram. A learner's complaint enters at the top and forks into subjective reactivity and objective reactivity. The subjective branch leads to a subtraction-and-observe loop; the objective branch leads to a clinician gate. A side panel shows the four-part pathophysiology model and a label panel strikes through the words that carry no standard.
steps: Entry point: a learner says their skin is sensitive, with three fields to record, timing (seconds, hours, days), distribution (only where applied, or elsewhere), and whether anything is visible.

Subjective branch: burning or stinging within seconds, no visible change, no spread; pathophysiological labels attached are neurosensory dysregulation and TRPV1 involvement; action is subtract to three steps and observe with three written fields for two weeks.

Objective branch: redness, scaling, swelling or rash, especially extending beyond the contact site or persisting for weeks; action arrow to a clinician for assessment that may include patch testing and objective measures such as transepidermal water loss.

Pathophysiology side panel: four boxes for impaired barrier function, inflammatory responses, neurosensory dysregulation and genetic predisposition, with foreign arrows for temperature change, pollution, ultraviolet exposure, hormonal fluctuation and psychological stress.

Application counter beside the loop: 11 products at 2 applications daily equals 154 weekly applications against 3 products at 2 daily equals 42, with the removed 112 highlighted, and the reduction described as the intervention.

Label panel: hypoallergenic struck through with the note that there are no federal standards or definitions, dermatologist tested and medical grade labelled no shared standard, and unscented flagged with the reminder that fragrance may be present to mask other odours, while fragrance-free is defined as no added fragrance or masking fragrance.

Reintroduction gate at the end of the loop: only after two stable weeks, one step at a time, with lesson 42's stop rule, and a red-flag lane listing eye involvement, facial or lip swelling, blistering, spread beyond the applied area, fever, or persistence beyond two weeks.

lessons.title: When a cosmetic routine is masking a medical problem: suppression, misattribution and delay
lessons.explanation: Some skin problems are not hidden by anything; they are hidden by the products applied to them. There are three distinct mechanisms, and naming them makes the boundary between cosmetic care and clinical care much easier to hold. The first is suppression. A product that quiets inflammation can reduce what the learner sees while the underlying process continues, and the clearest documented version of this is in the topical corticosteroid literature. The review used here describes the sequence skin passes through on topical steroid use as pre-atrophy, atrophy and then tachyphylaxis, with atrophy producing a burning sensation that further use soothes by vasoconstriction, and it describes the withdrawal pattern in which vasodilation follows and vessels become more dilated than they were initially, an effect the review calls a trampoline-like effect mediated through nitric oxide in the endothelium. The same review lists steroid rosacea, perioral dermatitis, steroid acne, skin atrophy with inhibition of keratinocyte proliferation and of collagen synthesis, telangiectasia, striae and a condition it calls status cosmeticus, described as an intolerance to cosmetics. Those findings concern prescription drugs used on the face, and the point for a learner is narrow and important: suppression changes appearance without resolving a cause, and the changes can include the skin becoming less tolerant of everything, which is why borrowed, imported or unlabelled creams that produce rapid improvement are a warning sign rather than a bargain. Public guidance reinforces the provenance problem, reporting that researchers have found steroids or mercury that were not listed on the label in skin-care products imported from other countries, and that prolonged unlabelled steroid use can thin and permanently discolour the skin. The second mechanism is misattribution, in which a condition is treated as a cosmetic complaint. Rosacea is the clearest example: the public description is a long-term inflammatory skin condition causing reddened skin and a rash, usually on the nose and cheeks, with symptoms that come and go and factors such as sun and emotional stress bringing them on; it describes several symptom types, including facial redness that may begin as a tendency to flush and persist for longer periods, sometimes with tingling or burning and rough scaly skin; red or pus-filled bumps that resemble acne; visible blood vessels; skin thickening, especially of the nose, which is described as one of the more severe symptoms and mostly affecting men; and eye irritation, with sore, red, itchy, watery or gritty eyes, swollen eyelids and styes. That source states plainly that eye symptoms require seeing a health care provider because untreated eye damage and loss of vision can result, that there is no cure but treatment can keep the condition under control, and that untreated skin may thicken and enlarge. It also notes that the condition may be underdiagnosed in darker-skinned people because darker skin can mask facial redness, which is a masking problem built into the skin rather than created by products. The third mechanism is delay by camouflage. Traffic in the opposite direction, from clinician to learner, matters just as much here: the national cancer institute explains that most adults have between 10 and 40 common moles, that melanoma can develop from a common mole or a dysplastic nevus but more often develops in an area of apparently normal skin, and that people with dysplastic nevi should be especially careful to protect their skin from the sun and avoid tanning and sunlamps. That combination is why a routine that conceals a changing spot, or a learner who believes that watching existing moles is sufficient, delays the one action that makes the biggest difference, which is having a change looked at. This lesson is education about recognising that boundary. It contains no diagnosis, no prescription and no advice to start or stop any treatment, and a prescribed treatment should be changed only by the prescriber.
lessons.example: Worked example. A learner has used a cream bought abroad for about six months for what she calls a stubborn red rash on the cheeks. It worked quickly, the redness returns whenever she stops, the skin now stings with everything, she has developed small visible vessels and a cluster of bumps, and she asks which barrier product will repair the damage. Work the sequence rather than the request. Step one, read the three mechanisms out of the history. Rapid improvement, return on withdrawal, thinning, visible vessels, and intolerance of previously tolerated products together match the described consequences of topical steroid use: pre-atrophy, atrophy and tachyphylaxis, a withdrawal pattern with rebound vasodilation, telangiectasia, steroid acne, and the intolerance the review calls status cosmeticus. Step two, count the exposure honestly so the delay is visible: about six months of twice-daily use is roughly 180 days and therefore about 360 applications, and the described consequences of prolonged use include thinning and permanent discolouration, which is time-dependent rather than reversible on demand. Step three, place the companion condition in the differential, because the bumps and flushing may also fit a rosacea-type picture, and the public description of that condition includes eye symptoms that require assessment to prevent damage. Step four, write the action. Nothing here is a barrier product: the action is to stop the unlabelled product only under clinical guidance, to bring the product itself or at least its name and origin to the appointment, to have the facial redness, vessels and bumps assessed, to answer questions about eye symptoms, and to keep the routine to a gentle fragrance-free cleanser, a plain moisturiser and photoprotection while that happens. Step five, model the arithmetic of delay in a different case to show why speed matters. A learner with a scaly patch on the ear that has been present for three months, that occasionally bleeds and is covered with concealer, has a different clock: the appropriate action is an appointment rather than a cream, because a lesion that does not heal, changes or bleeds is a clinical signal, and the concealer is the mechanism by which it went unexamined. Two cases, the same lesson: identify the mechanism, count the delay, and route the case.
lessons.question: A learner has used an unlabelled imported cream on her cheeks for six months; the redness returns whenever she stops, her skin now stings with everything, and she has visible vessels and new bumps. She asks for a barrier cream. What is the correct reading?
lessons.answer: This pattern matches suppression by an unlabelled product, with described atrophy, tachyphylaxis, rebound vasodilation, telangiectasia and intolerance of cosmetics, so the action is clinical assessment with the product details, not a barrier product, and any prescribed treatment changes only at the prescriber's direction
lessons.distractor: A barrier repair cream is the correct answer because the visible damage is a damaged skin barrier, and stopping the imported cream is unnecessary once the barrier is restored from the outside
lessons.correction: The topical steroid literature describes pre-atrophy, atrophy and tachyphylaxis, a withdrawal pattern with rebound vasodilation described as a trampoline-like effect, telangiectasia, steroid acne and an intolerance to cosmetics, and public guidance reports that imported products have been found to contain steroids or mercury that were not on the label, with prolonged use capable of thinning and permanently discolouring skin. A barrier product cannot undo those changes and does not address the returning inflammation; the essential steps are assessment, bringing the product details, and checking eye symptoms, because untreated eye involvement in the rosacea-type picture can cause damage.

depth.definitions: Suppression in this context means reducing visible inflammation or reactivity without resolving the process that produces it. Atrophy is thinning of skin, here through inhibition of keratinocyte proliferation in the epidermis and of collagen synthesis in the dermis. Tachyphylaxis is a diminishing response to a drug after repeated doses. Telangiectasia is visible dilated small blood vessels. Perioral dermatitis is an inflammatory eruption around the mouth. Steroid rosacea is a rosacea-like eruption attributable to topical steroid use. Status cosmeticus is a described intolerance to cosmetics. Rosacea itself is a long-term inflammatory condition causing reddened skin and a rash, usually on the nose and cheeks, with flares and remissions and no cure, though treatment can control it. A dysplastic nevus is an atypical mole. A non-healing lesion is a spot or sore that fails to heal, which is a clinical signal. Photoprotection means ultraviolet protection. 'Repair' as sold in marketing is not a regulatory category, and 'clinical strength' and 'medical grade' have no shared standard.
depth.mechanism: Suppression works by interrupting the signal rather than the cause, and the steroid literature shows what the interruption costs. Anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative actions reduce inflammation, which is experienced as improvement, while the same actions inhibit keratinocyte proliferation and collagen synthesis, so the epidermis thins and the dermis loses support; the review describes the sequence as pre-atrophy, atrophy and tachyphylaxis, notes that atrophy itself causes a burning sensation, and explains that further use soothes that burning by vasoconstriction, which is precisely the loop that keeps an unhelpful product in use. When use stops, the vasoconstriction reverses, and the review describes vasodilation overshooting the original vessel diameter, a rebound that looks like worsening disease and invites the learner to resume the product. Separately, a possible underlying condition may be present all along, which is why the rosacea description emphasises that symptoms come and go, that flushing may progress from occasional to persistent, that bumps may resemble acne, and that the process can thicken skin over time if untreated. Eye involvement is the part with the sharpest consequence, since the same source states that untreated eye damage and loss of vision can result. Delay by camouflage is the third mechanism and it operates on attention rather than on biology: covering a changing lesion or watching only existing moles changes when a change is noticed, and the national cancer institute's explanation that melanoma more often develops in apparently normal skin, alongside the figure that most adults have 10 to 40 common moles, is what makes a habit of covering and not checking costly. Two limits belong here. First, nothing in this mechanism says that a given learner's redness is caused by any particular product; appearance alone cannot establish a cause, which is why assessment exists. Second, no learner should start, stop or alter any prescribed medicine on the strength of this lesson, because withdrawal effects and treatment choices are prescriber decisions made with the person's full history.
depth.secondExample: Contrasting cases that a learner would describe in the same words. Case one: a learner whose acne has never been treated and who has started a prescription plan from a clinician, with expected peeling and dryness, and who hides the flaking with heavy makeup. Here nothing is masked in the harmful sense; the treatment is directed at the cause, the irritation is a known consequence, and the correct action is to follow the prescriber's instructions and raise concerns with them rather than to adjust cosmetics around it. Case two: a learner who uses a borrowed cream that produces rapid improvement, whose redness returns on stopping, and who has developed thinning and visible vessels. That is the suppression pattern, and the action is assessment with the product identified. Case three: a learner with persistent cheek redness and flushing plus gritty, watery eyes and a few bumps, who has been treating the whole picture as sensitive skin for a year. The eye symptoms alone justify an appointment, because untreated eye involvement carries described risk, and the facial picture needs assessment rather than more soothing products. Case four: a learner who has a mole on the back that has become darker and now itches, and who has decided to watch it because it does not look like the illustrations. The national cancer institute's point is that melanoma often arises in apparently normal skin, so the relevant question is not whether a mole matches a picture but whether a lesion is changing, and itch, bleeding or growth in a lesion is a reason to have it examined. Four presentations, four decisions, and in three of them the single most useful action is an appointment rather than a purchase.
depth.mistake: Four errors dominate. The first is treating improvement as evidence of safety, when a product that works quickly on a facial redness may be suppressing rather than resolving, and the rebound on stopping is then read as the problem returning rather than as the product's effect. The second is self-diagnosis by mirror, which converts a description into a certainty and skips the questions a clinician would ask, including about eyes, medicines, family history and the timing of each change. The third is the concealment habit, in which covering or working around a change becomes the whole plan, so the lesion is inspected less often than the rest of the face. The fourth is unilateral treatment change, stopping or continuing a prescribed medicine because of what a cosmetic routine seems to need; withdrawal patterns are described in the literature precisely because they are not benign, and they are managed by the prescriber. Diagnose your own reasoning with five questions. Did this improve quickly after starting a product whose full ingredients I can verify, and does it return on stopping? Is the pattern visible in places the product never touched, or is it confined to where it was applied? Is there any eye involvement, because that is the fastest route to harm? Is there a lesion that is changing, bleeding, itching or failing to heal, and is it being covered rather than examined? And is a prescribed treatment involved, in which case the next conversation is with the prescriber rather than with a shelf? Any of these triggers means clinical assessment, and this lesson contains no diagnosis and no treatment recommendation.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Audit your own routine for masking rather than for effectiveness, using a one-page record with five fields per product or lesion. Field one: the product and whether every ingredient on the label can be read and verified in a language and jurisdiction you can check, which is the provenance test that catches imported or borrowed creams. Field two: speed of visible improvement, because very fast improvement in a facial redness deserves a question rather than confidence. Field three: what happens when you stop, because return on withdrawal is information. Field four: whether the finding is confined to where you applied something or appears elsewhere. Field five: for any spot, sore, patch or mole, whether it is changing, bleeding, itching or failing to heal, and whether you currently cover it. Model response: 'Product A, local brand, all ingredients legible, gradual improvement over six weeks, no reaction on stopping, effects confined to application sites: keep. Product B, purchased abroad with a partial label and no ingredient translation, dramatic improvement in four days, redness returns within two days of stopping, small visible vessels have appeared: stop using and book an appointment, bringing a photograph of the label; no attempt to treat the withdrawal with another product. Spot on the left ear, scaly for three months, occasionally bleeds, currently covered with concealer: stop covering, photograph weekly with a ruler in frame, and book an appointment.' Self-review rubric, five points: every product is judged on verifiability, speed and stopping behaviour rather than on results alone; anything new, changing, bleeding, itching or non-healing has an appointment rather than a product; eye symptoms are recorded if present, because they change urgency; no prescribed treatment is altered, and any question about one is directed to the prescriber; and no entry claims a diagnosis, since the learner is recording observations for someone else to interpret. If you are taking a photo series of a lesion for a clinician, keep the lighting, distance and scale consistent, because change is only visible against a constant standard, and never delay an appointment in order to build a longer series.
depth.summary: A routine can mask three ways: by suppressing inflammation without resolving it, which the steroid literature shows through atrophy, tachyphylaxis, rebound vasodilation, telangiectasia and intolerance of cosmetics; by misattributing a condition such as rosacea, where eye symptoms carry real risk and darker skin can hide redness; and by delay through camouflage, where coverage and mole-watching substitute for examination even though melanoma often arises in normal-looking skin. Verifiability of the product, speed of improvement, behaviour on stopping, distribution, and lesion change are the five observations that decide the route, and prescriptions are only ever changed by the prescriber. The next lesson moves from what products hide to what they say, starting with the one section of a product that is regulated in its order: the ingredient list.

readings.title: Topical steroid-damaged skin, Indian J Dermatol 2014 (PMC4171912) — Introduction, 'Steroid Atrophy' (physiology and pathogenesis), 'Steroid-Induced Telangiectasia', 'Steroid Rosacea', 'Perioral Dermatitis', 'Tachyphylaxis' and 'Status Cosmeticus'
readings.note: Read the Introduction for the framing that topical steroids act as a double-edged sword because their anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative actions produce both therapeutic effect and side effects. Read 'Steroid Atrophy' for the described sequence of pre-atrophy, atrophy and tachyphylaxis, the burning sensation of atrophy, the soothing effect of vasoconstriction from further use, the stated inhibition of keratinocyte proliferation and of collagen synthesis, and the withdrawal pattern described as a trampoline-like effect through nitric oxide. Read the named sections for telangiectasia from abnormal capillary dilatation, steroid acne, steroid rosacea, perioral dermatitis, and 'Status Cosmeticus' described as an intolerance to cosmetics. This is a review of adverse effects of prescription topical corticosteroids used on the face, and it is cited here only to explain why suppression changes what a learner sees; this course contains no dosing, no prescribing, no instruction to start such a treatment, and no instruction to stop one, because withdrawal is managed by the prescriber.

readings.title: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases, Rosacea (niams.nih.gov) — 'Overview of Rosacea', 'Who Gets Rosacea?' and 'Symptoms of Rosacea'
readings.note: Read the Overview for the definition, the flare-and-remission pattern, the named triggers including sun and emotional stress, and the statement that there is no cure but treatment can keep it under control and usually combines self-care with medication. Read 'Who Gets Rosacea?' for the group profile and for the note that it may be underdiagnosed in darker-skinned people because darker skin can mask facial redness, which is the masking mechanism built into the skin itself. Read 'Symptoms of Rosacea' for the full symptom list used in this lesson, including redness that may begin as flushing and persist for longer periods with tingling or burning, red or pus-filled bumps resembling acne, visible blood vessels, skin thickening especially of the nose, and eye symptoms such as sore, red, itchy, watery or gritty eyes with swollen eyelids and styes. The page states that it is important to see a health care provider about eye symptoms because untreated eye damage and loss of vision can result, and that untreated skin may thicken and enlarge; these are the referral triggers quoted in this lesson. This page is also cited in lesson 52 for the 'Who Gets Rosacea?' section, where the reading purpose there was the midlife differential.

readings.title: National Cancer Institute, Common Moles, Dysplastic Nevi, and Risk of Melanoma (cancer.gov) — the opening definitions and the 'What should people do if they have a dysplastic nevus?' passage
readings.note: Read the opening for the two facts that support this lesson's delay argument: a common mole is a growth that develops when pigment cells grow in clusters, and most adults have between 10 and 40 common moles, usually above the waist on sun-exposed areas; and melanoma can develop from a common mole or dysplastic nevus but more often develops in an area of apparently normal skin. Read the passage beginning 'What should people do if they have a dysplastic nevus?' for the advice to protect the skin from the sun and avoid sunlamps and tanning booths, and note the page's framing that this is about risk rather than about self-diagnosis. This source is used only to justify the habit of having changes examined; no self-diagnostic rule is taught in this course.

lessons.title: Reading an ingredient list in order: what the law fixes, and where the information stops
lessons.explanation: The ingredient list is the only part of a cosmetic package whose order is set by regulation, which makes it the most reliable reading on the label and also the most over-read. Start with the rule itself. The federal regulation states that the label on each package of a cosmetic shall bear a declaration of the name of each ingredient in descending order of predominance, except that fragrance or flavour may be listed as fragrance or flavour, and it adds that no ingredient may be designated as fragrance or flavour unless it falls within the meaning of that term as commonly understood by consumers, and that where an ingredient has been accepted by the agency as exempt from public disclosure, the phrase 'and other ingredients' may stand in for it. A second paragraph supplies the alternative grouping that most large brands use: ingredients other than colour additives present at a concentration greater than one percent in descending order of predominance, followed by ingredients other than colour additives present at not more than one percent without respect to order, followed by colour additives without respect to order, with the option of folding the small-concentration ingredients into the descending list. The same paragraph structure also allows an ingredient that may or may not be present to be declared with the phrase 'may contain' under stated conditions. The public explanation of the requirement adds the administrative layer: retail cosmetics must list ingredients by their common or usual names, generally in descending order of predominance, under the Fair Packaging and Labeling Act, with the full requirements set out in the regulation; the declaration must be placed on an information panel where a consumer can find it; mail-order packages may instead carry instructions for locating the declaration, and distributors must respond promptly to requests; and because the Act applies only to consumer commodities, the requirement does not apply to products distributed only as free samples, for professional use, or for institutional use. Naming rules matter too. The agency does not accept botanical Latin names alone, European 'CI' colour numbers alone, or words from other languages such as Aqua and Parfum as substitutes for the common or usual name in English, but it does not object to those alternatives appearing in parentheses afterwards, which is why lists read Water (Aqua), Fragrance (Parfum) and Sweet Almond (Prunus Amygdalus Dulcis) Oil. Products that are both cosmetics and drugs, such as moisturisers carrying an SPF claim, must meet the requirements of both categories, which is why they also carry a drug facts panel with active ingredients named separately. Now the interpretive consequences, which are more useful than the rules themselves. The order tells you what is present in the greatest amount and nothing about how much: a product can be 70 percent water and still list an active fourth. Below the one percent line, order loses its meaning entirely by regulation, so a list of thirty ingredients may have twenty-five of them sitting in an unranked tail. Category words such as fragrance are legal shorthand for a mixture, so a single word on the label can stand for a group of substances, and the agency notes that even some products labelled unscented may contain fragrance ingredients added to mask the unpleasant smell of other ingredients. And a list says nothing about quality, safety or performance: it is a declaration of contents and order, not of effect. Marketing words such as clinical strength, medical grade, pharmaceutical grade and clean have no shared standard and should not be inferred from anything in the list. This lesson teaches how to read a regulated declaration. It contains no diagnosis, and an ingredient list cannot tell a learner whether a specific substance is causing their problem, because identifying a contact allergy requires clinical patch testing, and a suspected problem with a cosmetic can be reported to the regulator using the process described earlier in this course.
lessons.example: Worked example with two arithmetic checks. Two products both advertise 'with niacinamide'. Product A lists: Water, Glycerin, Niacinamide, Squalane, Cetearyl Alcohol, then twenty-eight further ingredients, ending with Parfum. Product B lists: Water, Glycerin, Caprylic/Capric Triglyceride, Cetearyl Alcohol, Niacinamide, then twenty-four further ingredients, with Fragrance appearing third. First, read the order. Niacinamide is third in A and fifth in B, so in A it sits above the humectant-and-emollient block and in B below it; the regulation's descending-order rule means A contains more niacinamide than B, and that is the only quantitative conclusion available. Nobody can say how much, and no comparison to a concentration claim is licensed by order alone. Second, work out why the tail cannot be read. Take a 30-gram bottle and suppose a 5 percent claim is accurate: 5 percent of 30 grams is 1.5 grams of the active in the whole tube, which is the scale of the thing being discussed. Now take a plausible composition for A: water at about 70 percent and glycerin at about 5 percent leaves 25 percent shared by the remaining 28 declared ingredients, which averages 0.89 percent each. Under the grouping rule, ingredients present at not more than one percent may be listed without respect to order, so those 28 entries could be in any sequence and the list would still comply, which means their positions carry no information at all. Third, read the fragrance entries. Product A ends with Parfum and Product B carries Fragrance in third position, which under the same descending-order rule is a real and useful difference: B's fragrance is present at a higher concentration than its niacinamide, and learners who react to fragrance have a reason to prefer A on that single point. Fourth, apply the provenance check from lesson 57: both lists are legible, in English, with parenthetical alternatives, which is what a compliant retail declaration looks like; a product whose list is partial, untranslated or absent cannot be read this way at all. Finish by writing down what the exercise does not establish. It does not establish that either product works, because order is not efficacy; it does not establish safety, because a declared ingredient list says nothing about how a person's skin will respond; and it does not identify a culprit, because that requires patch testing. What it does establish is which of the two contains more of the named active and which contains more fragrance, and those are two questions a learner can actually answer from the label.
lessons.question: Two moisturisers both say 'with niacinamide': product A lists Water, Glycerin, Niacinamide, Squalane and Parfum last, while product B lists Water, Glycerin, Caprylic/Capric Triglyceride, Cetearyl Alcohol, Niacinamide and Fragrance third. What can be concluded from the regulated order?
lessons.answer: A contains more niacinamide than B and B contains more fragrance than A, because ingredients are declared in descending order of predominance, while the concentrations and the efficacy of either product cannot be read from the list
lessons.distractor: Product A is the stronger and safer formulation because its active appears higher in the list, its fragrance is last, and a shorter distance between the active and the top of the list corresponds to a higher percentage of that active
lessons.correction: The regulation requires declaration in descending order of predominance, with fragrance or flavour permitted as category names and with ingredients present at not more than one percent allowed in any order under the alternative grouping. Order therefore supports a relative comparison of what is present in greater amount, which is why the niacinamide and fragrance positions are informative, and it supports nothing else: percentages are not disclosed, order is not a quality or safety signal, and a product that is mostly water can still list an active in fourth position. Efficacy and personal tolerance are not properties of a declaration of contents.

depth.definitions: An ingredient declaration is the list of contents required on retail cosmetics. Descending order of predominance means the greatest-amount ingredient is declared first. The one percent rule is the alternative grouping in which ingredients above one percent are listed in descending order, ingredients at or below one percent may be listed in any order, and colour additives are listed last. Fragrance and flavour are permitted category names rather than single substances. 'And other ingredients' is the phrase used where an ingredient is accepted as exempt from public disclosure. 'May contain' is permitted for an ingredient that may or may not be present under stated conditions. Common or usual name means the English name, with bracketed alternatives such as Aqua or Parfum allowed but not as substitutes. The International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients is the system whose names appear in those brackets. A cosmetic that is also a drug, such as a moisturiser with an SPF claim, must meet both sets of requirements and carries a drug facts panel listing active ingredients. Clinical strength, medical grade, pharmaceutical grade and clean are marketing phrases with no shared standard.
depth.mechanism: The regulation exists to make value and content comparisons possible rather than to describe performance, and understanding its purpose explains both its power and its edges. Because the declaration is ordered by amount, it answers the question a shopper actually has, which is which of two products contains more of the ingredient being advertised, and it does so without disclosing a formula, since a competitor cannot derive a percentage from a rank. The one percent clause is what makes this tolerable to manufacturers: below that line, exact order would disclose too much about a formula for little consumer benefit, so the tail is deliberately unranked, which is why long lists are informative at the top and silent at the bottom. The fragrance exception follows the same logic, because a fragrance is a mixture whose components are numerous and often proprietary, so the law permits one word to stand for the group while also requiring that the word be used honestly, meaning it may not be applied to something a consumer would not understand as a fragrance. The parental-naming convention solves a practical problem: the same substance has different names internationally, so the agency requires the common or usual name in English while allowing the harmonised alternative in brackets. Two consequences deserve emphasis because learners get them backwards. First, the list constrains marketing about contents, so a claim such as 'with vitamin C' must be true of a declared ingredient, but it places no constraint on whether that quantity does anything, because the law regulates labelling rather than effectiveness, and the same agency is explicit elsewhere that intended use decides whether a product is a cosmetic or a drug. Second, the one percent structural point means that the presence of an impressive-looking ingredient near the bottom of a long list is nearly uninformative, not because the ingredient is absent but because its position cannot be distinguished from that of twenty other ingredients sitting at similar concentrations.
depth.secondExample: Contrasting readings of the same list in different situations. Case one: a learner comparing two sunscreens by their drug facts panels rather than by their marketing, where the active ingredients are named with percentages and the inactive list follows the usual ordering. That is the one product category where percentages are on the package, which makes the comparison genuinely arithmetic rather than positional, and applying the tested-dose logic from lesson 37 to the cheaper of the two is a real decision. Case two: a learner who reacts to a cleanser and wants to know which ingredient is responsible, holding both lists side by side and looking for the substances that differ. That exercise narrows the field but cannot identify a cause, because the reaction may depend on concentration, on the combination, or on something not listed as a separate entry if it is part of a fragrance mixture; identifying the cause needs clinical patch testing, and the useful preparation is to bring the actual products rather than a photograph. Case three: a learner with dry skin comparing a body lotion whose first ingredient is water with one whose first ingredient is an oil, where the order immediately predicts a different sensory and occlusive profile and a different cost per gram. That is order being decisive, and it is exactly what the rule is for. Case four: a learner reading an imported product with a short, partial and untranslated list. Here the order is unreadable in the compliant sense, the absence of parenthetical common names is itself a signal that the label was not prepared for this market, and lesson 57's provenance test applies: if the contents cannot be verified, the product is a question for a clinician or the regulator rather than an entry in a routine.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first is treating the list as a strength grading, so that an ingredient in third position is taken to mean a specific percentage, or that a longer list is a stronger formula, when the regulation permits mostly water to occupy first place and an unranked tail to carry twenty ingredients at similar small concentrations. The second is reading safety from order, where a fragrance at the end is taken as proof of a gentle product and a fragrance near the top as proof of a bad one; the order tells you which contains more fragrance, while whether it irritates a given person is a different question answered by tolerance and, if needed, clinical testing. The third is the category illusion, in which words like clinical strength, medical grade, pharmaceutical grade, clean or dermatologist formulated are read out of the list; none has a shared standard, and the list contains no such information. The fourth is the misreading of absence, where a learner assumes a substance cannot be present because it is not named separately, when fragrance and flavour may be declared as categories, and when exemption provisions allow 'and other ingredients' and 'may contain' entries in defined circumstances. Diagnose your own reasoning with four questions. What is the actual question I am asking of this list, because order answers relative amount and nothing else? Is the ingredient I care about above or below where the one percent line plausibly falls, judged by the length and character of the entries before it? Is the product's declaration complete, legible and in a language I can verify, because if not, this lesson's reading method does not apply to it? And what am I refusing to conclude, namely efficacy, safety for my own skin, and the identity of a culprit, which are answered by evidence, by experience and by clinical assessment respectively?
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Take one product you already own and produce a one-page ingredient reading that does only what the regulation supports. Line one: transcribe the first five declared ingredients exactly, including bracketed alternatives, and state in plain language what each one is doing in the formula at that position. Line two: mark where the one percent line most plausibly sits and say why, using the character of the entries before and after it. Line three: record the fragrance entry, its name and its position, and note whether the product is labelled unscented, remembering that unscented products may contain fragrance added to mask other odours. Line four: note whether the package carries a drug facts panel, which would mean the product is both a cosmetic and a drug and that its active ingredients are named with percentages. Line five: write the two questions you would like the label to answer that it cannot, and where each would actually be answered. Model response: 'First five: Water, Glycerin, Niacinamide, Squalane, Cetearyl Alcohol; positions three and four are the named active and an emollient ester, which is consistent with the product's claim. One percent line: probably after position six, because positions one to six are water, a humectant, an active, an emollient, a fatty alcohol and a preservative system, and the remaining 24 entries are botanical extracts and thickeners. Fragrance: listed as Parfum at the very end, so fragrance is present at a low concentration relative to the rest; product is not labelled unscented. Drug facts panel: absent, so no active-ingredient percentages. Two questions the label cannot answer: whether the niacinamide amount does anything, which is a question for the evidence reviewed in lesson 43, and whether this product will irritate my skin, which is answered by a single-variable trial and, if a persistent reaction occurs, by clinical assessment.' Self-review rubric, five points: the transcription is exact and uses no paraphrasing of names; no percentage is invented for any ingredient; the fragrance entry is recorded with its position and its label wording; the drug-versus-cosmetic status of the package is stated from evidence on the package rather than assumed; and the closing questions are matched to the right sources of evidence rather than to a stronger product. Finally, note in the record what you would need to know to compare this product with another, which is the same five lines run on the second product, not a review site's summary of it.
depth.summary: The ingredient declaration is regulated in order, by amount, with fragrance and flavour permitted as category names, a one percent tail that may be listed in any sequence, and defined provisions for 'and other ingredients' and 'may contain'. That makes the list reliable for relative content at the top, uninformative in the tail, and silent on percentages, efficacy, safety and culpability. Read it as a declaration of contents, use the drug facts panel when the product is also a drug, and keep marketing adjectives such as clinical strength and clean where they belong, outside the regulated text. The next lesson turns to the sentences around the list, where claims of testing are made and where the standards change.

readings.title: 21 CFR 701.3, Designation of ingredients (Cornell Legal Information Institute copy of the eCFR text) — paragraphs (a), (f) and (g)
readings.note: Read paragraph (a) for the core rule quoted in this lesson: the label on each package of a cosmetic shall bear a declaration of the name of each ingredient in descending order of predominance, except that fragrance or flavour may be listed as fragrance or flavour, together with the conditions that an ingredient may not be designated fragrance or flavour unless it falls within the meaning commonly understood by consumers and the provision for 'and other ingredients' where an ingredient is exempt from public disclosure. Read paragraph (f) for the alternative grouping: ingredients other than colour additives present at a concentration greater than one percent in descending order, then ingredients other than colour additives present at not more than one percent without respect to order, then colour additives without respect to order, and the option to fold the small-concentration ingredients into the descending sequence. Read paragraph (g) for the 'may contain' provision. The eCFR page for the same section renders the opening of paragraph (a) but truncated its body when tested with text extraction; this Cornell copy returned the full text and is the version cited here.

readings.title: US Food and Drug Administration, Cosmetic Ingredient Names (fda.gov) — 'What the Law and Regulations Require: Overview', 'International Harmonization of Ingredient Names' and 'Products That Are Both Cosmetics and Drugs'
readings.note: Read the overview for the administrative detail used in this lesson: retail cosmetics must list ingredients by their common or usual names, generally in descending order of predominance, under the Fair Packaging and Labeling Act, with the requirements set out at 21 CFR 701.3; the declaration belongs on an information panel where a consumer can easily find it; mail-order products may instead carry instructions for locating it, and distributors must respond promptly to requests; and because the Act applies only to consumer commodities, the requirement does not apply to products distributed only as free samples, for professional use, or for institutional use. Read the harmonisation section for the naming convention and its limits, including that the agency does not accept Latin-only botanical names, European CI colour numbers or words from other languages such as Aqua and Parfum as substitutes for the common or usual English name, while not objecting to them in parentheses, with the examples Water (Aqua), Fragrance (Parfum), Honey (Mel), Sweet Almond (Prunus Amygdalus Dulcis) Oil and FD&C Yellow No. 5 (CI 19140). Read the third section for the rule that products which are both cosmetics and drugs, such as moisturisers marketed with SPF claims, must comply with both sets of requirements.

readings.title: US Food and Drug Administration, Cosmetics Labeling Guide (fda.gov) — the 'Ingredient Labeling' section: Prominence, Ingredient Identification, Order of Declaration, Fragrances and Flavors, Trade Secret Ingredients, Incidental Ingredients
readings.note: Read the list of headings on the page to see the shape of the requirement, then the 'Ingredient Labeling' subsections: Prominence, which requires the declaration to be prominent and conspicuous so it can be read and understood by ordinary individuals under normal conditions of purchase; Ingredient Identification, which refers to the naming requirement in 21 CFR 701.3(c); Order of Declaration, which restates the descending order of predominance rule and notes that exceptions are discussed later; and Fragrances and Flavors, Trade Secret Ingredients and Incidental Ingredients, which are the exceptions referred to. The page also explains what makes a cosmetic misbranded and lists the laws behind the requirements. This page and the Cosmetic Ingredient Names page together are the practical reading; the regulation text is the authority when the two are read side by side.

visual.title: Reading order: informative above the line, unranked below it, silent about effect
visual.description: A two-column label diagram. The left side draws a compliant ingredient list as a ladder with a one percent threshold line across it, above which order is meaningful and below which entries are shown in a shuffled heap. The right side shows the interpretive limits as a set of struck-through conclusions. A side box handles naming conventions and drug facts panels.
steps: Top rung: Water (Aqua) drawn largest, with a note that descending order of predominance begins here and that a formula may be predominantly water while still listing an active fourth.
Second and third rungs: glycerin and the named active shown in rank order, labelled the only quantitative comparison the list supports, namely which product contains more of the named ingredient.

Threshold line drawn across the ladder at the one percent mark, labelled from the grouped declaration rule, with the alternative grouping shown as greater-than-one-percent ingredients in descending order followed by not-more-than-one-percent ingredients without respect to order.

Below the line: a shuffled heap of 28 entries labelled botanical extracts, thickeners, preservatives and pH adjusters, with the caption that a 30 gram tube at a 5 percent claim holds 1.5 grams of active while the tail averages about 0.89 percent each, so position carries no information there.

Fragrance slot shown twice, once low on a list and once high, with the note that fragrance or flavour may be declared as a category, that one word may stand for a mixture, and that unscented products may still contain fragrance added to mask other odours.

lessons.title: 'Clinically proven': how to audit a product's claims about its own testing
lessons.explanation: Claims about testing are sentences, not evidence, and the useful skill is converting a sentence into a set of questions that have answers. Start with the legal frame, because it explains why some claims carry weight and others do not. The advertising regulator's guidance states that advertising must be truthful and not misleading and that, before disseminating an advertisement, advertisers must have adequate substantiation for all objective product claims conveyed expressly or by implication to consumers acting reasonably. It goes further for health-related products: as a general rule, claims about health benefits or safety require substantiation in the form of competent and reliable scientific evidence, and as a general matter substantiation of health-related benefits will need to be in the form of randomized, controlled human clinical testing. The guidance also sets out how reliability is judged, naming parameters such as sample size, duration and outcome measures that vary with the hypothesis and the accepted norms of the field, stating that assessing whether a study is well designed, well conducted and properly analysed are tasks for someone with appropriate expertise, and encouraging marketers to consult an independent expert. Two further features of that framework matter here. First, it covers implied claims, not only written ones; the guidance's own examples include images such as doctors in laboratory coats looking through microscopes alongside molecular structures and stacks of medical journals, which it says give an impression of scientific legitimacy and likely convey an implied claim that a product has been clinically proven. Second, it covers the whole of advertising, including packaging, brochures, digital content, social media and influencer marketing, press material and conference presentations, so a claim made by an influencer is advertising rather than commentary. The cosmetics regulator's other reach is narrower but equally useful: there are no federal standards or definitions governing the term hypoallergenic, the term means whatever a particular company wants it to mean, and manufacturers are not required to submit substantiation of hypoallergenicity claims to the agency; and whether a product is a cosmetic or a drug depends on its intended use, so a claim to treat or prevent disease, or to affect the structure or function of the body, shifts a product into the drug category and its evidence expectations with it. Practical auditing follows from those standards. A claim that can be audited names what was measured, in whom, how many people, for how long, against what comparison, and who paid. A claim that cannot be audited is usually a word rather than a finding, and the words recur: clinically proven, dermatologist tested, doctor recommended, clinical strength, pharmaceutical grade. Each has no shared standard, and each is doing the work of an evidence statement while providing none of its parts. This lesson is education about how to evaluate claims of testing. It contains no diagnosis and no treatment advice, and it does not tell anyone what to buy.
lessons.example: Worked example that audits three claim formats with arithmetic. Claim format one: '94 percent of 100 women agreed their skin looked smoother after four weeks.' Decompose it. The population is 100 women, and 94 percent of 100 is 94 women, so six disagreed; the outcome is agreement, which is self-assessment rather than a measured endpoint; there is no comparison group stated, so the counterfactual is unknown, and if the claim is really about satisfaction then a control group would be needed to show that 94 percent is higher than it would have been without the product. Now compute what one person is worth in a study that size: 1 divided by 100 is 1 percentage point, which means the headline number moves in whole points and that a hundred people cannot resolve small differences. Claim format two: 'in a clinical study of 32 participants over 8 weeks.' This one is auditable and should be audited rather than dismissed. The enrolled number is stated, so compute the resolution: 1 divided by 32 is about 3.1 percentage points, so a single participant's result moves the reported outcome by more than three points, which is a large step. Ask the next questions, namely what was measured (an instrument, a photograph scored blind, or a participant's opinion), against what comparison (a vehicle, another product, or nothing), and who funded and analysed it. A well-conducted 32-person study of one stated endpoint can be informative about that endpoint; a 32-person study with no comparison, a self-assessed endpoint and no statement about persistence is a demonstration rather than evidence. Claim format three: 'dermatologist tested, hypoallergenic and clinically proven.' This sentence can be audited to nothing, because the regulator states that there are no federal standards or definitions for hypoallergenic, that the term means whatever the company wants, and that substantiation need not be submitted; and because 'clinically proven' without a named endpoint, population and comparison is an unquantified assertion that the guidance treats as an implied efficacy claim requiring competent and reliable scientific evidence. Then apply the boundary that decides the whole exercise: if a product claims to treat acne, to lighten pigmentation or to remove scars, that is a drug-type intended use, and the comparison of interest is with the treatment a clinician would consider rather than with a rival moisturiser, which is exactly why those claims belong in a clinical conversation.
lessons.question: A product advertises '94% of 100 women agreed, dermatologist tested, clinically proven'. Which audit is correct?
lessons.answer: The panel figure describes self-assessment in 100 people with no stated comparison, the phrase clinically proven names no endpoint or design, dermatologist tested and hypoallergenic have no shared standard or substantiation requirement, and an efficacy claim of this kind would need competent and reliable scientific evidence from randomised controlled human testing
lessons.distractor: The panel of 100 makes the finding robust, and the term dermatologist tested confirms that the testing met a federal standard for substantiation, so the claims can be accepted as verified
lessons.correction: 94 percent of 100 women is 94 women agreeing and six not agreeing, with the outcome defined as agreement rather than a measured endpoint and no comparison group stated, so the counterfactual is unknown; one participant is worth one percentage point, which limits what a panel of that size can resolve. The advertising regulator requires adequate substantiation for objective claims expressed or implied, and for health-related benefits generally requires competent and reliable scientific evidence, as a general matter from randomized controlled human clinical testing. The cosmetics regulator also states that there are no federal standards or definitions governing hypoallergenic and no requirement to submit substantiation for it, so 'dermatologist tested' cannot be read as verified compliance.

depth.definitions: Substantiation is the evidence an advertiser must hold before making an objective claim. Competent and reliable scientific evidence is the standard the advertising regulator applies to health-related claims. A randomized controlled trial assigns participants by chance to different conditions, which is what allows differences to be attributed to the intervention. A control condition is the comparison, which may be a placebo or vehicle, an existing treatment, or waitlist. An endpoint is the specific thing measured; a self-assessment endpoint is a participant's opinion or rating, while an instrument-based endpoint is a measurement. Blinding means participants, assessors or both do not know which condition was received. Implied claims are meanings a reasonable consumer takes from an advertisement even if not written, such as the impression created by images of laboratory settings. Intended use is what determines whether a product is a cosmetic or a drug in the United States. There are no federal standards or definitions for hypoallergenic, dermatologist tested, doctor recommended, clinical strength or pharmaceutical grade, and all are marketing language rather than evidence terms.
depth.mechanism: The reason evidence has a structure is that a causal claim needs an answer to the question of what would have happened otherwise, and only a comparison can supply it. A single group followed over time measures change, but change over weeks includes regression to the mean for fluctuating problems, seasonal effects, concurrent routine changes and the ordinary wishful perception of one's own face in a mirror; a control group is what separates the intervention from those other causes. Randomisation addresses the problem that people who choose a product differ systematically from those who do not, in severity, motivation and habits. Blinding addresses the fact that expectations change both perception and reported outcomes, which is why a self-assessed endpoint without blinding is weak evidence even when the sample is large. Sample size sets the resolution: with 100 participants one person is one percentage point, and with 32 participants one person is about 3.1 percentage points, so small studies can only detect large effects. Duration and follow-up answer whether an effect persists, which matters because many cosmetic effects are transient. Funding and analysis matter because judgement enters at many points, including which endpoint is chosen, which results are reported and how missing data are handled, which is why the guidance suggests consulting an independent expert rather than adjudicating design questions alone. The honest limit is that this framework tells a learner how to rank claims, not how to conduct a trial or how to decide what to use; and for anything with a drug-type intended use, including acne, pigmentation and scarring, the relevant comparison is with clinical management rather than with a competitor product.
depth.secondExample: Contrasting claim audits in a learner's own shopping list. Case one: a learner who responds to 'clinically proven' by buying the most expensive product in the category. The audit produces no endpoint, no population, no comparison and no sample size, so the money is being spent on an unquantified assertion, and the alternative is to buy for a job in the routine from lesson 41 and to judge the product on the learner's own observation, which is honest and cheap. Case two: a learner who reads a named study of 40 people over 12 weeks comparing the product with its own vehicle, and requests the results summary. That claim can be audited, and the appropriate response is to ask whether the measured difference was visible, whether it persisted, and whether the participants' skin resembles the learner's, which is where the population matters. Case three: a learner who wants a product for actively inflamed acne and who is comparing serums on the strength of influencer reviews, which the guidance treats as advertising. The category confusion is the important part here, since acne is a condition with clinician management, and the relevant claim audit is whether the plan addresses the follicular process described in lesson 38 under clinical supervision, not which serum has the better testimonial. Case four: a learner who reacts badly to a product and wants a remedy from the claim language. Nothing in the claims helps; the useful steps are the exposure map and report process from lesson 42, and clinical assessment if the reaction is persistent, spreading or severe.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first is treating a named number as evidence without the structure around it, so that '94 percent of participants' is accepted as proof of effect when nothing states what the comparison was or what was measured. The second is the reverse error, dismissing any study that is small, when the correct reading of a 32-person study depends on the endpoint and the comparison rather than on the number alone; size limits resolution and does not by itself invalidate a result. The third is category confusion, where drug-type claims to treat acne, pigmentation or scarring are evaluated as if they were cosmetic preference claims, which removes the clinical comparison that would matter. The fourth is label shorthand, where hypoallergenic, dermatologist tested and doctor recommended are treated as regulated certifications when no federal standards or definitions govern them and no substantiation has to be submitted. Diagnose your own reasoning with five questions. What exactly is being claimed: a sensation, an appearance, a measured property, or a treatment for a condition? In whom and how many, and what does one participant move in percentage points? Compared with what, and was the comparison blinded? For how long, and did the effect persist after the product stopped? And who funded, conducted and analysed it, because an answer of 'unspecified' is an answer about the claim's strength even when the product itself is fine? Any claim to treat a condition moves the decision to a clinician, and no claim in this lesson's scope changes a prescribed treatment.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Build a claim audit card for one product you are considering, with six rows and a verdict line. Row one: transcribe the strongest single claim verbatim from the packaging or the advertisement. Row two: classify it, as a sensation, an appearance claim, a measured property or a treatment for a condition. Row three: extract the parts that are present, namely what was measured, how many people, for how long, against what comparison and who funded it, and mark each part present or absent. Row four: compute the resolution if a number of participants is given, by dividing 1 by that number and expressing it in percentage points. Row five: flag the words with no shared standard that appear anywhere in the wording, including clinically proven, dermatologist tested, doctor recommended, clinical strength, pharmaceutical grade and hypoallergenic. Row six: state what would change your mind, in terms of a specified endpoint over a specified window. Model response: 'Claim: clinically proven to reduce the appearance of fine lines in 8 weeks. Classification: appearance claim. Parts present: duration, eight weeks. Parts absent: what was measured, how many people, comparison, funding. Resolution: not computable, no participant number given. Words with no shared standard: clinically proven. What would change my mind: a stated endpoint such as blinded photographic scoring or a measured wrinkle parameter, a stated sample size, a stated comparison condition and a stated persistence check.' Self-review rubric, five points: the claim is quoted rather than paraphrased; every missing element is recorded as missing rather than inferred; the percentage-point resolution is computed rather than guessed whenever a sample size is present; no claim to treat a condition is treated as a cosmetic claim; and the verdict distinguishes between 'unable to audit' and 'shown to be false', because most weak claims fail the first test rather than the second. Keep the card with the routine audit from lesson 41 so the purchase decision is made on a stated job and a stated observation.
depth.summary: Claims about testing can be audited against a defined standard: objective claims require adequate substantiation, health-related benefits generally require competent and reliable scientific evidence and, as a general matter, randomized controlled human clinical testing, and reliability is judged on parameters including sample size, duration and outcome measures, including implied claims created by imagery and by influencer content. Audit the parts, compute the resolution, flag the words with no shared standard, and route drug-type claims about conditions to clinical care. That completes the toolkit; the final lesson assembles it, for one person with one stated set of constraints.

Read the examples about implied claims, including the laboratory-coat imagery used in this lesson to explain why pictures count as claims.

readings.title: US Food and Drug Administration, Cosmetics Safety Q&A: 'Hypoallergenic' (fda.gov)
readings.note: Read the answer for the three statements this lesson relies on: hypoallergenic cosmetics are products that manufacturers claim produce fewer allergic reactions than other cosmetic products; there are no federal standards or definitions that govern the use of the term, and it means whatever a particular company wants it to mean; and manufacturers of cosmetics labelled hypoallergenic are not required to submit substantiation of their hypoallergenicity claims to the agency, with dermatologists reported as saying the term has very little meaning. This page is the clearest single counterexample to the assumption that a product label implies verified testing.

visual.title: From claim sentence to audit card, with the resolution arithmetic
visual.description: A conversion diagram. On the left, three claim sentences are decomposed through a funnel into five labelled parts. On the right, an audit card is drawn with a resolution calculator and a flag strip for words with no shared standard. A footer routes drug-type claims to clinical care.
steps: Funnel input, three sentences: '94 percent of 100 women agreed their skin looked smoother', 'in a clinical study of 32 participants over 8 weeks', and 'dermatologist tested, hypoallergenic, clinically proven'.
Funnel stages, five labelled parts: what was measured; in whom and how many; for how long; against what comparison; and who funded and analysed it, each marked present or absent for each sentence.

Resolution calculator panel: one participant in 100 equals 1 percentage point, so the panel cannot resolve fine differences; one participant in 32 equals about 3.1 points, so a single result moves the headline by more than three points; labelled as the reason sample size is a parameter rather than a verdict.

Endpoint distinction panel: self-assessment against instrument-based measurement, with the note that expectation changes reported outcomes when participants are not blinded, and that a comparison condition is what supplies the counterfactual.
