lessons.title: Capstone: one constraint set, one minimal routine, and the arithmetic that proves it fits
lessons.explanation: This lesson assembles the whole level by building one routine for one stated person, and the constraint set is deliberately the awkward kind. The person is 34, works outdoors for about six hours a day including the middle of the day, has dry skin that stings easily with many products, has reacted to fragranced products before, has roughly twelve dollars a month for skincare, has about four minutes in the morning, and washes dishes most evenings, so their hands are wet again at the end of the day. There is no diagnosed skin condition and no prescribed treatment. Start with the jobs, because the plan is jobs rather than products: cleanse without stripping, replace water and lipid, and protect from ultraviolet radiation during the hours of exposure, with a treatment slot that stays empty because nothing has been prescribed. Public guidance on application order gives the sequence for the face as washing, then any treatment, then moisturiser and sunscreen, and it states plainly that using too many products may irritate the skin, particularly when more than one anti-ageing product is in play, and that this irritation can make the very signs a learner is trying to reduce more noticeable. For this person that warning is not theoretical, since reactivity is part of the constraint set: the routine must be small enough that any reaction is attributable. Then design against the constraints in order. Tolerance first, so every step is fragrance-free and the plan contains no exfoliant and no active while the baseline is being established. Cost second, and here the interesting failure appears, because the arithmetic changes depending on where the moisturiser is used. Sun protection third, because a person who works outdoors for six hours in the middle of the day has the largest cumulative exposure in this level's examples, and occupational guidance for outdoor workers points to scheduling, shade and training as well as personal protection. Water and lipid replacement fourth, because it is what keeps the tolerance plan comfortable. The trial comes last and contains exactly one variable. Two obligations complete the plan: the arithmetic must be shown, so the plan is checkable rather than aspirational, and the clinical thresholds must be written down, because a routine is not a route for a condition. This is education. The prices used below are illustrative units chosen to make the arithmetic visible, not recommendations, and any practitioner treating a condition, any prescribed product, and any new, changing or non-healing lesion sits outside this exercise entirely.
lessons.example: Worked capstone with the arithmetic shown at every step. Product A, a gentle fragrance-free cleanser, costs 12 dollars for 236 millilitres; at 2 millilitres a day that is 118 days of supply, 3.09 units a year and about 37 dollars a year. Product B, the same plain emollient moisturiser for face and hands, costs 16 dollars for 454 grams; at 3 grams a day for the face alone that is 151 days, 2.41 units and about 39 dollars a year. Product C, a broad-spectrum water-resistant sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher, costs 14 dollars for 88 millilitres; at the tested-dose benchmark of about 1.2 grams for the face, that is 73 days, 4.98 units and about 70 dollars a year, or 438 grams of sunscreen across the year. The first version of the plan therefore comes to about 145 dollars a year, which is 12.12 dollars a month and fits the twelve-dollar budget almost exactly, and it delivers five applications a day, or about 1,825 application events a year, in roughly four minutes each morning and about 24 hours across the year. Now introduce the constraint that the budget did not anticipate: the hands. Six hand washes a day at 1 gram of moisturiser each adds 6 grams daily rather than 3, which halves the days of supply to about 76 and raises moisturiser cost from 39 dollars to about 77 dollars, taking the annual total to about 184 dollars, or 15.33 dollars a month, which breaks the budget by roughly three dollars a month. Solve it with the arithmetic rather than with hope, and solve it without touching protection. There are three legitimate moves: consolidate, so the same emollient is bought in the largest size available and decanted into two containers, which improves cost per gram without changing what is used; reallocate deliberately, keeping the sunscreen at full dose on face, ears, neck and the backs of the hands while using a cheaper plain emollient for the body and dishwashing-adjacent hand care; and reduce the count of unnecessary products to zero, which is what already frees the budget, since the nine-step version of this routine would have cost the same twelve dollars a month before any of it was replaced. Serving suggestions about brand names are not part of the exercise; the point is that the arithmetic exposes the binding constraint and that protection is the last thing sacrificed. Then write the trial and the boundaries. Trial: one variable, swapping the current fragranced cleanser for the fragrance-free one, fourteen days, recording seconds of stinging after washing and minutes of tightness, with a stop rule for burning over a minute or a rash beyond the washed area. Boundaries: no exfoliant, no active, no imported or unlabelled product, no change to any prescription, and clinical assessment for a lesion that changes or will not heal, eye symptoms, facial swelling, or a rash that persists beyond two weeks of gentle care.
lessons.question: A 34-year-old outdoor worker with reactive, dry skin and a twelve-dollar monthly budget has a three-product plan costing about 145 dollars a year, but adding hand use of the moisturiser raises it to about 184 dollars, or 15.33 dollars a month. What is the defensible resolution?
lessons.answer: Consolidate and reallocate rather than cut protection, keeping the sunscreen at full dose on exposed sites and moving body and hand care to the cheapest plain emollient that does the same job, with one variable under trial and every clinical threshold written down
lessons.distractor: Reduce the sunscreen to the amount that fits the budget and drop the moisturiser to a single evening application, since protection can be stretched and the routine's cost is the constraint that matters most
lessons.correction: The cost arithmetic is real: at 6 grams a day for hands as well as face, days of supply halve to about 76 and moisturiser cost rises from about 39 dollars to about 77 dollars a year, taking the total to about 184 dollars or 15.33 dollars a month. The response that survives scrutiny is consolidation, larger sizes and deliberate allocation, because ultraviolet exposure is the one input in this plan that keeps accumulating across the year and cannot be recovered later. The trial still changes one variable at a time, and because there is reactivity in the constraint set, the plan contains no exfoliant, no active and no unverifiable product.

depth.definitions: A constraint set is the list of limits a plan must respect: budget, time, climate, occupation, tolerance and any clinical condition. The four jobs are cleansing, active treatment (only if a clinician has prescribed one), moisturising and lipid replacement, and photoprotection. Cost per year is unit price divided by size, multiplied by daily dose, multiplied by 365; days of supply is size divided by daily dose. Adherence is whether the plan actually happens on an ordinary day, which is why time and cost are part of the design rather than afterthoughts. A substitution rule means a new step replaces an existing one. A stop rule is the evidence, written in advance, that ends a trial. Clinical stewardship means a prescribed treatment is left exactly as prescribed and its questions go to the prescriber. A provisional plan is one designed to be adjusted at a stated review point rather than held as a verdict. Fragrance-free means no added fragrance or masking fragrance. The products named in this lesson are illustrative price points used to demonstrate arithmetic, not recommendations.
depth.mechanism: Constraints bind in a fixed order, and getting that order right is what makes a minimal routine minimal. Tolerance comes first, because a step that irritates cannot be sustained and irritation itself changes what every other observation means. Cost comes second, because a routine that consumes more product than the budget allows will be abandoned, and an abandoned routine produces no data; the same logic applies to time, since a plan that needs fifteen minutes on a working morning is a plan for weekends only. Protection comes third, because it is the only step whose effect is measured against a cumulative exposure that keeps accumulating. Water and lipid replacement come fourth, because they make daily life comfortable and improve how the other steps are tolerated. Active treatment, if any, sits outside this ordering entirely, because a prescriber's instructions govern it. The arithmetic that makes the ordering concrete is straightforward and worth doing for any plan. Divide 1 by the sample size to get the resolution of any evidence claim, divide size by daily dose to get days of supply, multiply through to get annual cost, and count reapplication events for a shift outdoors. Then design against the binding constraint rather than against an ideal. In the example below the binding constraint turns out to be the budget once the hands use the same product as the face, and the resolution is not to cut protection but to consolidate products and change how much is used where. Two limits belong with the method. First, illustrative prices show the arithmetic and not the market, so a learner re-runs the same formulas with their own shelf prices. Second, a capstone routine cannot absorb a condition: if acne, eczema, rosacea, a pigmentary disorder, a new or changing lesion or persistent unexplained symptoms are present, the routine is adjunctive and the clinical plan is primary, and nothing in this lesson diagnoses or treats anything.
depth.secondExample: Same skeleton, three different constraint sets. Constraint set one is the one worked in the example: outdoor work, reactive skin, about twelve dollars a month, four minutes in the morning, fragrance sensitivity. The answer is three products with one used at two sites, protection kept at full dose, and no actives. Constraint set two: a 68-year-old with mature, dry, non-reactive skin, no fragrance sensitivity, a twenty-five dollar monthly budget and plenty of time, who has never had a routine and finds long lists off-putting. The skeleton is identical, but the product choices shift: a richer occlusive moisturiser becomes the centre of the plan because the measured change is water loss and reduced lipid content, the cleanser can be a moisturising bar rather than a liquid, and the plan adds the skin-examination habit because the public guidance notes that skin-cancer risk rises from around age 50. What does not change is the number of jobs, the daily photoprotection, or the rule about one change at a time. Constraint set three: a 19-year-old with active, scarring acne, oily skin, and a wish to buy five products at once. Here the capstone refuses to be the plan. Acne is a condition with clinician management described earlier in this course; the routine supports the clinical plan with a gentle cleanser, one moisturiser and photoprotection, and every additional step waits until the condition is being managed. Three constraint sets, one skeleton, and the discipline of naming the binding constraint is what produces three different but equally defensible plans.
depth.mistake: Four errors appear whenever a capstone is attempted. The first is designing for an ideal week rather than an ordinary one, which produces a plan that fails on the third workday and then gets judged as a personal failure. The second is solving a cost problem by cutting protection, when protection is the step with the cumulative exposure behind it; the correct moves are consolidation, dose discipline, and cheaper vehicles that do the same job. The third is importing a condition into a cosmetic plan, so that acne, a persistent rash or a changing lesion is folded into a routine instead of routed to a clinician, which delays the one action that matters. The fourth is the final flourish, adding one more product at the end because the plan looks too simple, which reintroduces the attribution problem the whole construction was designed to avoid. Diagnose your own plan with five questions. Does every step name a job that no other step performs? Does the annual cost, computed from real package sizes and your actual dose, fit the budget every month rather than in a good month? Does the plan survive an ordinary weekday in the time available? Is there exactly one variable under test at a time, with the observations and the stop rule written before starting? And is anything present that should have stopped the exercise, namely a condition, a changing lesion, eye symptoms, or a prescribed treatment whose instructions are not being followed? If the last answer is yes, the plan's next step is a clinician rather than a shelf.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Produce a one-page capstone plan for one person with one stated constraint set, and write it as a document someone else could audit. Section one: the constraints, stated numerically, namely monthly budget, minutes available, climate and indoor environment, occupation and exposures, tolerance observations, and any clinical condition or prescription. Section two: the jobs, one line each, with the step that performs it and the reason it cannot be removed. Section three: the arithmetic, showing days of supply, units per year and annual cost for each step, plus a reapplication count if the person works outdoors, and the monthly total compared with the budget. Section four: the trial, naming the single variable under test, the window, the observations and the stop rule. Section five: what is deliberately not included, with the reason for each exclusion. Section six: the clinical thresholds, including any prescription rule and any symptom that ends self-directed care. Model response excerpt: 'Constraints: 12 dollars a month, 4 minutes in the morning, 6 hours outdoors on workdays, fragrance-sensitive, no diagnosed condition, no prescription. Jobs: cleanse once in the evening and rinse in the morning; moisturise face twice daily and hands after every wash with the same plain product; protect with one broad-spectrum water-resistant SPF 30 or higher, reapplied every two hours outdoors. Arithmetic: cleanser at 2 mL a day gives 118 days a bottle, 3.09 bottles a year, 37 dollars; moisturiser at 3 g a day gives 151 days, 2.41 units, 39 dollars, rising to 77 dollars if the hands use 6 g; sunscreen at 1.2 g a day gives 73 days, 4.98 bottles, 70 dollars; the three-step version totals about 145 dollars a year, or about 12 dollars a month, which fits. Trial: one variable, swapping the cleanser for a fragrance-free one, 14 days, recording stinging seconds after washing and tightness minutes, with a stop rule for burning over one minute or any rash beyond the washed area. Not included: exfoliant, any active, masks, devices, because the routine has no job for them yet. Clinical thresholds: stop and seek assessment for a facial rash with swelling, eye symptoms, a lesion that changes or will not heal, or any prescribed treatment question.' Self-review rubric, five points: the constraints are numeric so the plan can be checked; every step names a job; the arithmetic is computed from stated sizes and doses and compared with the budget rather than assumed; exactly one variable is under trial with a written stop rule; and the exclusion list and clinical thresholds are present, which is what separates a plan from a wish list. Review the plan after four weeks and change at most one thing.
depth.summary: A minimal routine is a set of jobs under stated constraints, and the capstone is the discipline of naming the constraint that binds, doing the arithmetic so the plan fits an ordinary month, changing one variable at a time, and holding three boundaries: conditions and changing lesions route to clinical care, prescriptions are governed by the prescriber, and unsupported words never enter the plan. The same skeleton serves a reactive outdoor worker, a mature first-time user and a teenager with acne, and only the products and the clinical weighting differ. That is where this level ends and where the parent's integration of the whole course begins.

readings.title: American Academy of Dermatology, Should I apply my skin care products in a certain order? (aad.org) — the numbered steps and the 'too many products' paragraph
readings.note: Read the four numbered steps, which are the skeleton of this capstone: wash, apply treatment if there is one, apply moisturiser and/or sunscreen, then makeup. Read the paragraph above them stating that using too many products may irritate the skin, particularly when more than one anti-ageing product is in use, and that the irritation can make the signs a learner is trying to reduce more noticeable; that sentence is why this plan contains no actives while the baseline is being established. This page is also cited in lesson 41, where the reading purpose was the job structure of a routine and the stability argument; here the purpose is the capstone's application sequence, so read it for the order itself and for the note on the crescent area around the eyes.

readings.title: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, NIOSH, Sun Exposure at Work (cdc.gov) — 'Overview', 'Reducing risk' and 'Treating a sunburn'
readings.note: Read the Overview for the figures that make sun protection the non-negotiable step in this capstone: outdoor work in sunlight increases the risk of sunburn and skin cancer, exposure is highest in summer and between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., snow and light-coloured sand reflect ultraviolet so rays reach exposed skin from above and below, and workers are at risk even on cloudy days. Read 'Reducing risk' for the measures that belong to a workplace rather than to a person, namely scheduling work when there is less sunlight exposure, providing shaded or indoor break areas, and training workers about exposure and its signs, since a plan that only changes what a worker applies leaves the strongest lever untouched. Note that this page names a minimum of SPF 15, while dermatology public guidance recommends SPF 30 or higher; this course states both and attributes each rather than harmonising them silently. This page is also cited in lesson 54, where the reading purpose was the exposure mechanism and the photosensitivity list. This NIOSH page returns HTTP 403 to scripted requests, so it was read with a text-extraction tool rather than curl; the sections named here were confirmed in the extracted text when this pack was authored, and a reader should open it in a browser to see the full page.

readings.title: Federal Trade Commission, Health Products Compliance Guidance (ftc.gov) — the substantiation standard, read here as the plan's purchase filter
readings.note: Re-read the passage stating that objective claims must be substantiated before an advertisement is disseminated, that health-related claims require competent and reliable scientific evidence, and that as a general matter substantiation of health-related benefits will need to be in the form of randomized, controlled human clinical testing, with reliability judged on parameters such as sample size, duration and outcome measures. In this lesson the passage functions as a buying filter rather than as a research method: with a twelve-dollar monthly budget and four minutes in the morning, an unauditable claim is not a reason to spend, because the plan already names the job each step performs. This page is also cited in lesson 59, where the reading purpose was claim auditing; here the purpose is the filter applied at the point of purchase.

visual.title: Capstone: constraints in, jobs out, arithmetic checked, boundaries held
visual.description: A single-page plan diagram. Constraints enter from the left as numeric boxes. In the centre, four job slots are filled by three products, with a trial slot and one empty treatment slot. On the right, a cost ledger computes days of supply and annual cost and compares two scenarios against the budget. A boundary strip runs along the bottom.
steps: Constraint column, numeric: 12 dollars a month; 4 minutes in the morning; 6 hours outdoors including midday; wet hands each evening; fragrance sensitivity; no diagnosis and no prescription.

Job column, four slots: cleanse without stripping; treat (empty, because nothing is prescribed); moisturise and replace lipid; protect against ultraviolet radiation, with the protection slot marked non-negotiable because exposure accumulates.

Product substitution arrows: one fragrance-free cleanser, one plain emollient used at two sites, one broad-spectrum water-resistant sunscreen, and a crossed-out list of exfoliants, actives, masks and devices with the reason that no job is waiting for them.

Cost ledger, scenario one: cleanser 12 dollars for 236 millilitres at 2 millilitres a day gives 118 days, 3.09 units and 37 dollars a year; moisturiser 16 dollars for 454 grams at 3 grams a day gives 151 days, 2.41 units and 39 dollars; sunscreen 14 dollars for 88 millilitres at 1.2 grams a day gives 73 days, 4.98 units and 70 dollars; total about 145 dollars a year, about 12.12 dollars a month, which fits.

Cost ledger, scenario two: hand use raises the moisturiser to 6 grams a day, halving days of supply to about 76 and raising its cost to about 77 dollars, so the total becomes about 184 dollars a year, about 15.33 dollars a month, which breaks the budget by roughly three dollars; the resolution arrows show consolidation, larger sizes and reallocation, never a cut to protection.

Trial slot with a single arrow: one variable, the fragrance-free cleanser swap, 14 days, observations of stinging seconds after washing and tightness minutes, stop rule for burning over one minute or a rash beyond the washed area.

Effective-dose and exposure strip: about 438 grams of sunscreen a year at 1.2 grams a day for the face, four applications across a six-hour shift at two-hourly intervals, and the counted annual application total for the three-step routine against a nine-step comparison.

Boundary strip along the bottom: no exfoliant or active during baseline; no imported or unlabelled product; no change to any prescription; and clinical assessment for a new, changing or non-healing lesion, eye symptoms, facial swelling, or a rash persisting beyond two weeks of gentle care.

questions.prompt: A learner burns within seconds of using many products with no visible change, owns eleven products, and asks which hypoallergenic sensitive-skin line to switch to. What is the best-supported plan?
questions.answer: Subtract to three steps so the weekly application count drops sharply, observe for two weeks with written fields, and treat hypoallergenic and sensitive-skin wording as unstandardised, with clinical assessment if visible signs, spread or persistence appear
questions.distractor: Switch the whole shelf to hypoallergenic sensitive-skin products, because that label identifies formulations whose allergens were removed and whose testing was submitted for review
questions.correction: The regulator states that there are no federal standards or definitions governing hypoallergenic, that the term means whatever a company wants it to mean, and that manufacturers need not submit substantiation. Sensitive skin is described as a syndrome of discomfort to normally innocuous stimuli with sensory, barrier and inflammatory components, so the first intervention is reducing exposures: eleven products at two applications a day is 154 weekly applications against 42 for three products, a difference of about 112 weekly and about 224 across a fortnight. Visible, spreading or persistent signs are the ones that require a clinician, because contact allergy and inflammatory conditions can present in exactly this way.

questions.prompt: A learner used an unlabelled cream bought abroad for six months; the redness returns within two days of stopping, the skin now stings with everything, and there are new bumps and small visible vessels. She asks which barrier product will repair it. What is the correct reading?
questions.answer: The history matches suppression with described atrophy, tachyphylaxis and rebound vasodilation, so the action is clinical assessment with the product details and a check for eye symptoms, while any barrier product is not the intervention
questions.distractor: A barrier repair cream is the answer because the stinging shows a damaged barrier, and once the barrier is restored the underlying redness will settle without further assessment
questions.correction: The topical steroid literature describes pre-atrophy, atrophy and tachyphylaxis, a withdrawal pattern in which vasodilation overshoots the original vessel diameter, telangiectasia, acneiform eruptions and an intolerance of cosmetics, and public guidance reports undeclared steroids or mercury in imported skin-care products, with prolonged use capable of thinning and permanently discolouring skin. Those changes are not reversed from the outside, and the returning redness is not evidence of an unfinished barrier repair. Any prescribed treatment is a prescriber's decision, and eye involvement is the fastest route to harm in a facial inflammatory picture.

questions.prompt: Two moisturisers both say 'with niacinamide'. Product A lists Water, Glycerin, Niacinamide, Squalane, Parfum last; product B lists Water, Glycerin, Caprylic/Capric Triglyceride, Cetearyl Alcohol, Niacinamide, Fragrance third, and B also carries an SPF claim. What can be concluded and what must not be?
questions.answer: A contains more niacinamide and B contains more fragrance because declaration follows descending order of predominance, while percentages, efficacy and personal tolerance cannot be read from the list, and B's SPF claim means it must meet both cosmetic and drug requirements with active ingredients named on a drug facts panel
questions.distractor: A is the stronger and gentler choice because its active sits higher and its fragrance sits last, and B's SPF claim shows the product was tested to a single standard that covers both categories
questions.correction: The regulation requires declaration in descending order of predominance, permits fragrance or flavour as category names, and allows ingredients present at not more than one percent to be listed without respect to order under the alternative grouping, so order supports only a relative comparison of amount and not a percentage. In a 30 gram tube a 5 percent claim corresponds to 1.5 grams of active in total, and a plausible tail of 28 ingredients sharing 25 percent averages about 0.89 percent each, which is why tail positions are uninformative. Products that are both cosmetics and drugs, such as a moisturiser with an SPF claim, must comply with the requirements of both categories, which is why the drug facts panel appears. Efficacy is answered by evidence and personal tolerance by a single-variable trial, not by rank.

questions.prompt: A product claims '94% of 100 women agreed, dermatologist tested, clinically proven' and the learner wants to know whether it will help their acne scars. Which evaluation is correct?
questions.answer: The panel is self-assessment in 100 people with no stated comparison, the assurance words carry no shared standard or substantiation duty, and a claim about scars is a drug-type intended use that belongs in a clinical conversation rather than in a cosmetic comparison
questions.distractor: The panel size of 100 is large enough to make the result reliable and the dermatologist-tested wording confirms third-party verification, so the product can be evaluated alongside clinical options
questions.correction: 94 percent of 100 women is 94 agreeing and six not agreeing, with the outcome defined as agreement, no comparison group and therefore no counterfactual, and one participant worth one percentage point. The advertising regulator requires adequate substantiation for objective claims expressed or implied and, for health-related benefits, competent and reliable scientific evidence, generally from randomized controlled human clinical testing judged on parameters such as sample size, duration and outcome measures; the cosmetics regulator states that no federal standards govern hypoallergenic and no substantiation must be submitted. Scars are a structural tissue change, so the relevant comparison is clinical management, not a rival serum.

questions.prompt: A 34-year-old outdoor worker with reactive dry skin and a 12 dollar monthly budget finds their three-product plan costs about 145 dollars a year, rising to about 184 dollars when the same moisturiser is also used on the hands. What should change?
questions.answer: Consolidate, buy the largest sizes and allocate deliberately between face, hands and body so that the sunscreen dose stays intact, and keep the plan to one variable under trial with the clinical thresholds written down
questions.distractor: Reduce the sunscreen dose and apply the moisturiser only at night, because the two most expensive steps are the ones that must absorb the budget shortfall
questions.correction: At 6 grams a day rather than 3 the moisturiser's days of supply halve from about 151 to about 76 and its annual cost rises from about 39 dollars to about 77 dollars, which is the whole of the overspend; the arithmetic makes the binding constraint visible. Ultraviolet exposure is the one input that accumulates irreversibly, so protection is the last step to reduce, and cheaper plain emollients can do the same body and hand job at a lower cost per gram. Reactivity in the constraint set means no exfoliant and no active while the baseline is established, since using too many products may irritate skin and make the signs being targeted more noticeable.

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old asks you to rank four products that promise to reverse thinning, and mentions that since November the same products sting, their shins crack, and the house is heated all day. Separately, a friend says a humidifier and cooler showers fixed the same complaint. Construct the reasoning that decides what to do first.
questions.answer: Treat the seasonal variables as the first coherent intervention because indoor air in winter holds far less water, map each product to whether a topical step can reach the measured change, and add nothing until the seasonal group has been held constant for two weeks
questions.distractor: Rank the four products by the strength of their anti-ageing claims, add the strongest immediately, and treat the seasonal complaint as a separate dryness problem that the products will address once they take effect
questions.correction: Ageing changes are thinner epidermis, reduced lipid content, lower glandular output and loss of dermal collagen and elastin, and a topical step reaches hydration, barrier function, tolerance and protection only, so no product addresses the dermal framework and no ranking exercise is meaningful. Winter indoor air at room temperature holds about 11.0 grams of water per cubic metre at 60 percent relative humidity against about 4.6 at 25 percent, roughly 58 percent less, so the physical driver is larger before anything is applied. Shorter warm washing, a gentle cleanser, emollient on damp skin and humidification form one coherent group that can change together, whereas products follow the one-variable rule because the season itself is already a variable.

questions.prompt: A 51-year-old has itchy, dry, sometimes eczematous skin that began when her cycles became irregular. She has used the same fragranced body wash for ten years, has recently started a new laundry detergent, and asks about a phytoestrogen serum. Design the reasoning and the observation plan.
questions.answer: Log across about three cycles with rated symptoms and every competing change, treat the long-used fragranced wash and the new detergent as live suspects, start with the documented general measures, and leave the phytoestrogen serum alone because no topical step changes circulating hormone levels
questions.distractor: Start the phytoestrogen serum, because the timing of her cycles makes hormonal change the explanation, and a topical product that supports oestrogen activity can substitute for the falling levels in her skin
questions.correction: Oestrogen receptors are distributed through skin with the highest density on the face, genital region and legs, and falling oestrogen is associated with higher transepidermal water loss and reduced dermal collagen, but those are systemic changes and the reported repair signal comes from clinician-directed treatment rather than cosmetics; 'hormonal' and 'balancing' have no shared standard. The most commonly reported perimenopausal dermatoses are eczematous eruptions and itching with dryness, and both long-standing fragranced products and new detergents are plausible contact or irritant causes. A 28-day cycle means about 3.2 cycles fit in 90 days, and two cycles is only 56 days, which is the minimum window for reading a cyclic pattern.

questions.prompt: A learner with deep brown skin presents three problems: flat brown marks from old acne, acne that still flares, and a raised firm nodule at an old piercing site that sometimes itches. She asks which of two serums to buy and whether to scrub first. Build the full plan and justify each element.
questions.answer: Treat and prevent the inflammation driving the marks, protect with a tinted iron-oxide broad-spectrum sunscreen and expect months with possible new marks, keep the routine gentle because irritation adds pigment, buy neither serum until the driver is addressed, and have the raised nodule assessed clinically
questions.distractor: Use the stronger serum and scrub first to lift the surface pigment, because the marks sit in the epidermis and accelerating turnover is how pigment is removed, and flatten the nodule with the serum as well
questions.correction: Pigment follows inflammation through mediators that raise melanocyte activity, so scrubbing is a fresh inflammatory stimulus, and where basal keratinocytes have been damaged the pigment sits in the dermis in melanophages and clears slowly, which is why response to topical care differs by depth. Public guidance begins with sunscreen, specifically a tinted product with iron oxide for visible light plus SPF 30 or higher and broad-spectrum coverage, and states that marks are treatable but not curable because new ones can form. A raised scar that extends beyond the original injury is a different tissue with reported incidence in darker-pigmented populations of 4.5 to 16 percent and higher risk in pregnancy and puberty; it belongs to a clinician, and imported products have been found to contain undeclared steroids and mercury capable of thinning and permanently discolouring skin.

questions.prompt: A dishwasher in a restaurant washes their hands about fifty times a shift, wears gloves for long unbroken periods, and has deep painful cracks. A landscape gardener colleague burns on cloudy days and takes a diuretic. Compare the two exposure problems and set out the actions that follow for each.
questions.answer: For the dishwasher, reduce the counted wetting and glove exposure at source and use a plain emollient after every wash with clinical assessment because painful cracks are a red flag; for the gardener, treat medication-related photosensitivity, the peak window and reflection as the drivers, keep full-dose protection and have any non-healing lesion examined
questions.distractor: For both, the answer is a stronger protective product: a barrier cream that can withstand fifty washes a day for the dishwasher and a high-SPF cream for the gardener, since both problems are failures of product strength rather than of exposure
questions.correction: Fifty wetting events a shift is over ten thousand a year, so exposure reduction at source dominates, and gloves worn for long unbroken periods macerate the skin while latex proteins and rubber accelerators can sensitise, which is why glove material, dryness before donning and duration are the questions. The pooled prevention figures come from low-quality evidence with intervals crossing the line of no effect, and the public guidance states that hand eczema looks like dry skin but needs more than a good moisturiser, that it tends to worsen without treatment and preventive measures, and that painful, extremely dry hands failing to respond to moisturising warrant assessment. For the gardener, outdoor work raises skin-cancer risk, exposure peaks between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., snow and light-coloured sand reflect radiation, cloud does not eliminate it, and listed medicines including thiazides, diuretics and certain antibiotics and anti-inflammatories increase photosensitivity.

questions.prompt: A learner reports burning within seconds of applying most products, no visible change, and a shelf of eleven items. Three weeks later the same learner reports a red, scaly rash spreading from the jaw to the cheeks that began after a new hair dye. Explain how one case becomes two and what each requires.
questions.answer: The first is a subjective sensory pattern addressed by subtracting to three steps and observing with written fields, while the second has visible signs and a distribution beyond the contact site, which requires clinical assessment because identifying a contact allergen needs patch testing
questions.distractor: Both are the same sensitive-skin problem and both are addressed by the same approach, namely switching every product to a hypoallergenic sensitive-skin range and waiting for the barrier to recover
questions.correction: Sensitive skin is a syndrome of discomfort to usually innocuous stimuli with sensory, barrier and inflammatory components, and the discriminator is whether anything is visible and whether it spreads; the sensory pattern is treated with reduction, which takes eleven products and 154 weekly applications down to three products and 42, while the visible spreading rash is a clinician's problem. Regulator statements matter for the shopping response: there are no federal standards or definitions governing hypoallergenic, the term means whatever a company wants it to mean, and substantiation need not be submitted, so a new range carries no assurance. Hair dye is a recognised source of contact allergy, the allergen is identified by clinical patch testing, and the useful preparation is to bring the products rather than a photograph.

questions.prompt: A learner uses a borrowed unlabelled cream for facial redness and notices rapid improvement, thinning skin, new visible vessels and, on any attempt to stop, more redness than before. Their clinician had separately prescribed a treatment for a diagnosed condition, which the learner has been alternating with the borrowed cream. Set out the reasoning and the obligations.
questions.answer: Recognise suppression with described atrophy, tachyphylaxis and rebound vasodilation, stop the borrowed product only under clinical guidance with the product details available, keep the prescribed treatment exactly as the prescriber set it, and report eye symptoms immediately because untreated eye involvement can cause damage
questions.distractor: Continue the borrowed cream because it works faster than the prescribed treatment, and stop the prescription while the skin recovers, since improvement is the best available evidence of what is helping
questions.correction: The steroid literature describes pre-atrophy, atrophy and tachyphylaxis, a withdrawal pattern in which vasodilation overshoots the original vessel diameter, telangiectasia, acneiform lesions and an intolerance of cosmetics, and public guidance reports undeclared steroids or mercury in imported products with thinning and permanent discolouration as consequences. Rapid improvement followed by rebound on stopping is a described signature rather than reassurance. Prescribed treatment is a prescriber decision and never a learner's, and the described facial condition includes eye symptoms for which the guidance states that a health care provider should be seen because untreated eye damage and loss of vision can result. Concealing a change with makeup is the delay mechanism, so the plan is assessment with the products in hand.

questions.prompt: A learner compares two sunscreens. One is a cosmetic-only moisturiser with 'with vitamin C' and a long ingredient list; the other carries an SPF 50 claim, a drug facts panel and a water-resistance statement. They also want to know how much to use. Explain how to read both packages and how to convert the protection claim into a dose.
questions.answer: Treat the SPF product as both cosmetic and drug so its active ingredients are named with percentages on the drug facts panel, read the cosmetic list only for relative amount above the one percent line and for fragrance position, and convert protection into the tested-dose benchmark of about 1.2 grams for the face with reapplication every two hours outdoors or after swimming and sweating
questions.distractor: Read both lists the same way and choose the one with the named ingredient higher up, then use a pea-sized amount because SPF already describes how much protection the product gives
questions.correction: The regulation requires declaration in descending order of predominance with the alternative grouping that leaves ingredients at or below one percent unranked, so order supports relative comparison only; the one place percentages appear is the drug facts panel of a product that is also a drug. A 30 gram tube holds 1.5 grams of active at a 5 percent claim and a tail of 28 ingredients averaging about 0.89 percent each, which is why rank cannot be read as strength. The tested-dose benchmark is about 2 milligrams per square centimetre, which is roughly 1.2 grams for a face of about 600 square centimetres and about 438 grams across a year of daily use, and the blocked fraction runs 1 minus 1 divided by SPF, so SPF 30 blocks about 96.67 percent and SPF 50 about 98 percent; the difference is small in percentage points but real in transmitted dose, and it is only realised at the tested dose with reapplication. Sunscreen label claims such as waterproof and sweatproof are not permitted; water-resistant is the term the regulator allows.

questions.prompt: Three advertisements arrive in one week: one reports that 94 percent of 100 participants agreed their skin looked smoother, one reports a study of 32 participants over 8 weeks against a vehicle, and one says dermatologist tested, hypoallergenic, clinically proven. Rank what can be concluded and design the purchase decision that follows.
questions.answer: The vehicle-controlled study is the only auditable one and prompts questions about endpoint, blinding, persistence and funding, the 100-person panel describes self-assessment with no comparison at a resolution of one point per participant, and the third states nothing auditable because the assurance words carry no shared standard or substantiation duty
questions.distractor: The 100-person panel ranks first because 100 is the largest number, the 32-person study ranks last because small studies cannot be informative, and the assurance words confirm that the third product met federal substantiation requirements
questions.correction: The advertising regulator requires adequate substantiation for objective claims expressed or implied, with health-related benefits generally requiring competent and reliable scientific evidence and, as a general matter, randomized controlled human clinical testing judged on parameters including sample size, duration and outcome measures, and it treats imagery of laboratory settings as potentially conveying an implied claim. Resolution arithmetic follows from the sample: one participant in 100 is one percentage point, while one participant in 32 is about 3.1 points, so the 32-person study is limited in precision but not automatically invalid, and what matters is whether it compared with a vehicle, measured a stated endpoint, blinded the assessors and reported persistence. The cosmetics regulator states that no federal standards or definitions govern hypoallergenic and that manufacturers need not submit substantiation, so assurance wording cannot rank above a study. The purchase decision belongs to a named job in the routine, an observable endpoint over a stated window, and one variable at a time.

questions.prompt: Build one routine for a 34-year-old outdoor worker with reactive dry skin, a twelve-dollar monthly budget, four minutes each morning and wet hands every evening, and state what would have to be true for a fourth step to be added.
questions.answer: Three steps covering cleanse, moisturise and protect, with the sunscreen at full dose and the same plain emollient allocated across face, hands and body by size and cost, no exfoliant or active while the baseline is established, and a fourth step admitted only when it replaces an existing one or fills an unmet job after two stable weeks
questions.distractor: Four steps selected by claim strength, with an exfoliant for texture and a serum for dryness added at the start because a plan must cover every skin concern before it can be considered complete
questions.correction: The four jobs are cleansing, treatment if one is prescribed, moisturising and photoprotection, and this person has no prescription, so three products cover the plan. The arithmetic is decisive: at 2 millilitres a day the cleanser gives about 118 days and 37 dollars a year, at 3 grams a day the moisturiser gives about 151 days and 39 dollars, and at 1.2 grams a day the sunscreen gives about 73 days and 70 dollars, totalling about 145 dollars or 12.12 dollars a month; hand use raises the moisturiser to about 77 dollars and the total to about 184 dollars, so consolidation and allocation solve the gap while protection stays intact. Public guidance warns that using too many products may irritate skin, particularly when more than one anti-ageing product is in use, and that this can make the signs being targeted more noticeable, which matters because reactivity is part of this constraint set. A new step earns its place by replacing a step or filling a job, one variable at a time, with a stop rule written in advance.

questions.prompt: A learner in a hot, humid city notices oiliness, breakouts on the back and a wet face after a daily cycle commute, and decides to drop sunscreen and add an exfoliant and a heavier night cream. Explain what the climate actually changes and what it does not change.
questions.answer: Humid heat raises sweat hours, residue and friction, so lighter vehicles, gentler and less frequent cleansing and changing out of wet clothing are the adjustments, while photoprotection stays in place and the exfoliant is deferred because adding it alongside two other changes destroys attribution
questions.distractor: Humid heat means the skin is already hydrated, so sunscreen and moisturiser become unnecessary and the routine should shift entirely towards oil control with an exfoliant and a drying mask
questions.correction: Sweat changes what the skin surface is doing: measured transepidermal water loss on the forearm rose from 8.6 to 59.4 grams per square metre per hour after six minutes of cycling, about 6.9 times, and the reviewed conclusion is that the sweat component cannot be separated from true barrier function without deactivating the glands, so a wet face is not evidence of a hydrated barrier. Air holding more water reduces the vapour-pressure gradient for water loss, but it does not reduce ultraviolet exposure, and low-intensity and incidental exposure accumulates, which is why protection is the step that stays. Adding an exfoliant and a heavier night cream in the same week as dropping sunscreen introduces three variables and an unjustified reduction in the only step with a cumulative downstream cost; irritation also raises the risk of new pigment in skin that tans easily. One climate variable, one coherent adjustment group, one product change at most.

questions.prompt: A learner in their 60s is proud of a nine-step routine, has a new dark spot on the cheek that they cover with concealer, has not had a skin examination, and reports that a moisturiser marketed for mature skin has made their skin sting. Assemble the review of this whole situation.
questions.answer: Reduce the routine so the total insult falls, have the new dark spot examined rather than covered, begin the skin-check habit that the risk profile warrants, and re-map the products to the measured changes of mature skin so that hydration, barrier support and protection replace steps that promise collagen reconstruction
questions.distractor: Increase the routine to address each complaint separately with a lightening product for the spot, a calming product for the stinging, and two more products for the ageing concerns, since thoroughness is the best protection
questions.correction: The measured changes of mature skin are a thinner epidermis, reduced lipid content, fewer active glands and loss of dermal collagen and elastin, and a topical step reaches hydration, barrier function, tolerance and photoprotection only, so adding steps does not address the changes being complained about, while using too many products may irritate skin and make the signs being targeted more noticeable. A new, changing, bleeding or non-healing lesion is a clinical signal and coverage reduces the chance of noticing change, and the public guidance notes that skin-cancer risk rises from around age 50, which makes examination a habit rather than a response. Marketing terms aimed at this age group, including age-defying and clinically proven, carry no shared standard, and stinging with a new moisturiser is a reason to subtract it rather than layer a calming product on top.

questions.prompt: A learner asks you to combine everything from this level into one decision about a single new product they want to buy: it is expensive, sold through an influencer who demonstrates results, claims to treat acne marks and uneven tone, comes in a package whose ingredient list is partly illegible, and the learner also has active acne that is starting to scar. Set out the complete reasoning.
questions.answer: Decline the purchase for now: the claim to treat marks is a drug-type intended use, the illegible list fails the provenance test, influencer demonstration is advertising with implied claims requiring substantiation, and active scarring acne is a condition whose management takes priority, with the routine limited to a gentle cleanser, one moisturiser and photoprotection alongside that clinical plan
questions.distractor: Buy it and use it alongside the rest of the routine, because a product that demonstrates visible results in a video is stronger evidence than a study summary, and the marks are cosmetic once the acne itself has been treated
questions.correction: Under the advertising regulator's framework, objective claims expressed or implied require adequate substantiation before dissemination, health-related claims generally require competent and reliable scientific evidence from randomized controlled human clinical testing, and influencer content is advertising, so a demonstration is not a substitute for an endpoint, a comparison, a sample size or a duration. A partly illegible list cannot be read by the regulated order rule, and public guidance reports undeclared steroids or mercury in imported products with thinning and permanent discolouration as consequences, so the provenance test applies. A claim to treat marks is a drug-type intended use and belongs in a clinical conversation, and acne that is beginning to scar is explicitly a reason to treat the condition rather than to add cosmetic steps, since marks recur while the driver runs and scarring is structural. The supportable routine while that happens is a gentle cleanser, one moisturiser and daily photoprotection, with one variable at a time and a written stop rule.
